articles.title: Vance walks Trump tightrope with scathing election critique blaming Iran war
articles.snippet: The vice-president's blunt assessment of Republican election defeat marked one of the sharpest breaks with a sitting president in recent memory.
articles.full_text:
Vance walks Trump tightrope with scathing election critique blaming Iran war
- Published
Vice-President JD Vance sent shockwaves through Washington on Wednesday by blaming his party's midterm defeat squarely on the Iran war, in what was widely interpreted as an effort to distance himself from President Donald Trump ahead of a potential 2028 White House run.
In a carefully calibrated, 600-word statement on X, the vice-president acknowledged that Trump's 2024 voters had deserted Republicans in the midterm election.
"The reason we lost is the war," he wrote. "The president himself said so last night."
In interviews late Tuesday night and Wednesday, Trump had defended the war but acknowledged that it played a factor in Democrats flipping control of the US House of Representatives and the Senate.
Vance's view on the war in Iran is an open secret in Washington. While he has repeatedly backed the conflict since the US and Israel attacked Tehran in February, he has reportedly expressed opposition in private meetings with administration officials.
But those disagreements had been kept out of the public eye - until now.
Hours after Trump and the party were handed a bruising election defeat, Vance made clear that he felt the decision to go to war was a clear political mistake.
"If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest," Vance said.
It was a striking statement, and one with no recent precedent: it's hard to recall a similar moment in recent US political history when a sitting vice-president has so sharply broken with the president on a signature foreign policy issue.
Then came an arguably even greater surprise: Trump - who typically demands steadfast loyalty from his senior advisers - agreed with Vance that the midterms were "largely" decided by the war. He added that he would "do it again" if given the same choices.
It was an early sign that Trump - who has prized loyalty from his advisers - may give Vance a wide berth should he choose to launch a presidential campaign.
"I know how he feels about it. I think it was -- I think it was fine," Trump told reporters when asked about Vance's post blaming the war. "I knew that when I went in, and we stopped them from having a nuclear weapon, and they will never have a nuclear weapon."
Vance's statement seemed like "a way of separating himself from Trump," said Daniel Byman, a foreign policy expert at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
Drawing contrasts with Trump will be a delicate balancing act if Vance seeks the presidency, Byman added.
That balance was on display in Vance's post. The vice president didn't mention Trump by name and attributed much of his election results analysis to unnamed pollsters.
Vance "put his toe in the water to see what he's going to do," Ashley Davis, a Republican strategist, told the BBC.
Beyond the Iran war criticism, Vance also offered a political roadmap that could preview a possible presidential campaign. He distilled the party's strategy to win back voters into a neat four-point gameplan: "1) End the war 2) Focus on cost of living/inflation 3) Put America First 4) Change our relationship to Israel."
The list encapsulated much of Vance's worldview since bursting onto the national political scene, and read like the core argument in a future stump speech.
The BBC has contacted Vance's office for comment.
Of course, the next presidential election is still two years away. Vance is expected to run but hasn't made an official decision, and aides insist that he's still mulling it over.
It's also up for debate exactly how much Vance broke from Trump. Vance showed the message to Trump before posting it online, according to The New York Times.
Trump, for his part, could change his mind and make clear he'll brook no dissent from Vance or anyone else.
The president has been circumspect about who he'd support to succeed him as the 2028 Republican presidential nominee. Trump has praised Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio on several occasions, but hasn't said when - or if â he'd make an endorsement.
The president appears to relish the guessing game of who he'd back to carry on his political movement, even in the past floating the idea that he'd continue to a third term (which is barred by the US Constitution).
Vance's midterms missive might not be that significant in the end. Or it could have been the starting gun for the 2028 race and the battle for the post-Trump Republican Party.
Nardine Saad contributed reporting.

articles.title: French protests see numbers surge as unions join strikes over high cost of living
articles.snippet: The interior ministry estimates 600,000 people joined protests across France, while the unions say the number was far higher.
articles.full_text:
French protests see numbers surge as unions join strikes over high cost of living
- Published
More than 600,000 protesters have taken part in rallies and marches across France, according to France's interior ministry, with five unions joining a day of action demanding more money for wages and public services.
The left-wing CGT union put the number of people taking part in Thursday's mobilisation at 1.57 million and hailed the figure as "a level unmatched" since 2023, citing big protests in Paris, Marseille, Bordeaux and Lille.
As darkness fell in Paris, Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu said he would convene a "social conference" with unions and employers next Monday.
The wave of protests began in September over poor conditions and resources at lycÃ©es (high schools), before spreading to universities, workers and a revived "yellow-vest" movement against high prices.
The unions had vowed to take the co-ordinated move against the government "to the next level", and CGT chief Sophie Binet had said their message was that "the only thing that will bring this mobilisation to a halt is responding to our demands".
Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez had earlier deployed 70,000 police, vowing "an extremely firm response" to any potential outbreaks of violence.
Some unrest was reported in several cities.
A car was set alight near the Gallieni bridge over the RhÃ´ne river in Lyon, as hundreds of activists from the radical left-wing "black bloc" clashed with police.
Clashes were also reported in the north-western city of Rennes, where the local prefect said a "hostile group of masked individuals" had gathered in front of the main union march. Tear gas was used to clear a square in the south-western city of Bordeaux and a teenager was hurt in a stabbing involving a student at a high-school blockade in the Seine-Saint-Denis suburb of northern Paris.
But the trouble was not on the scale seen during the last big day of protests, on Saturday 17 October, when more than 2,000 stores were looted and historic buildings set on fire.
The provisional numbers reported on Thursday were higher than on 17 October, considered the biggest day of rallies until now when the interior ministry said 550,000 people had turned out and the unions counted 800,000.
Earlier on Thursday the leader of the CFDT union, Marylise LÃ©on, said she would be happy if the protests matched that earlier level.
A coalition of unions across the public and private sector had urged workers, pensioners and young people to join Thursday's day of strikes to intensify pressure on the government. In particular they are seeking a rise in the minimum wage, or Smic, which is currently â¬12.31 (Â£10) an hour.
Sophie Binet told reporters at the start of a march in central Paris that protesters had "just reached a new level in their mobilisation" and were demanding immediate answers.
An estimated 9.89% of civil servants were taking part in the strikes, according to government figures.
Disruption was reported in schools, hospitals and public transport, and the Eiffel Tower and some exhibition rooms at the Louvre museum in Paris had to close.
Workers were also asked to halt production at oil refineries and France was expected to import more electricity than it produced on Thursday because of disruption at nuclear plants.
The head of the CFDT complained that it was not just the minimum wage that needed to increase. "We are asking for a net increase of â¬100 a month," Marylise LÃ©on explained.
The government has sought to appease public anger over rising prices, bringing down the cost of fuel by releasing 10 million barrels of diesel from strategic reserves. Ministers have also promised school students to reform the unpopular Parcoursup university admissions platform and eventually replace it by 2028.
The prime minister said early on Thursday evening that Monday's "social conference" with unions and employers would seek to "provide answers to questions surrounding purchasing power and wages".
However, the government by its own admission has little room to manoeuvre, as it looks to make tens of billions of euros in savings, in a bid to cut the budget deficit to 5% of GDP.
The education ministry said that 16% of teachers had gone on strike on Thursday, and the unions said disruption had affected more than one in four lycÃ©es, which cater for 15-18 year-olds, as well as the vast majority of universities.
"Now it's not only about [investing in] public services in education and higher education, it's about all of the public services in France," the vice-president of the Unef student union, Alice De Brito, told the BBC.
Meanwhile, a revived gilets jaunes (yellow-vest) movement that staged a revolt against the high cost of living several years ago has called for further blockades and protests on Friday and Saturday too.
Thursday's march was eventually allowed in central Paris, although not along the route proposed by the unions between Place de la Bastille and Place de la Concorde, which would have taken protesters near the National Assembly, the ÃlysÃ©e Palace, and the prime minister's residence at HÃ´tel Matignon.
Instead, the march followed another central route from Place de la RÃ©publique to Place de la Nation.
The interior minister had earlier spoken of three potential risks on Thursday, from radical left "black blocs" groups and looting to wildcat marches without union authorisation.

articles.title: Paraguay President Santiago Peña resigns after bank collapse
articles.snippet: The move follows a bank collapse and after the lower house of congress voted in favour of pursuing an impeachment trial against him.
articles.full_text:
Paraguay President Santiago PeÃ±a resigns after bank collapse
- Published
Paraguay's President Santiago PeÃ±a has announced his resignation following a political crisis sparked by the collapse of a bank linked to him.
"I want to apologise to the people if at any point I failed," he said in a video message on social media. "It was never my intention to betray the trust you placed in me."
The crisis erupted after Ueno Bank entered an insolvency process, which froze all operations. Lawmakers accused PeÃ±a, who was a shareholder until last year in the company that owned the bank, of conflicts of interest and misconduct.
PeÃ±a has rejected suggestions of impropriety. His resignation comes after Paraguay's lower house of congress voted in favour of pursuing an impeachment trial.
In his video message posted on X, PeÃ±a said his resignation was to protect stability, social peace and democratic institutions.
Ueno Bank has said it has about three million customers, equivalent to about 60% of Paraguay's adult population.
It held pensions and some other public funds and, after its collapse earlier this week, millions could not access their accounts.
The central bank seized the digital lender, and people took to the streets protesting and demanding PeÃ±a's resignation.
A new president of the Central Bank of Paraguay has been appointed and Congress has approved a process to pay depositors.
PeÃ±a won election in 2023 representing Paraguay's ruling conservative Colorado Party, beating a centre-left challenger.

articles.title: Paraguay President Pena resigns in wake of bank collapse
articles.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera
articles.snippet: President Pena, a Trump ally, had faced an impeachment motion and protests after the collapse of digital lender ueno.
articles.full_text:
Paraguay President Pena resigns in wake of bank collapse
Paraguayan President Santiago Pena resigned on Thursday after calls for his removal swelled following the collapse of digital lender ueno that left millions of customers unable to access their accounts.
“I do so with the stability of our country, social peace and the need to preserve our democratic institutions in mind,” he said in a video recorded address on Thursday.
Pena, an ally of US President Donald Trump, is stepping down after the opposition called an extraordinary session to begin the process of filing an impeachment motion in Congress, and as protesters demanded his resignation.
Earlier on Thursday Pena lost backing from members of his own conservative party. Vice President Pedro Alliana is set to take office as his replacement.
Lawmakers had accused Pena of conflicts of interest, misuse of pension funds and institutional cover-ups linked to the collapse of ueno, which had grown quickly from a niche fintech player into a mid-tier bank administering close to $850 million in public funds.
“He is accused of negligence at the very least and complicity in covering up the fact that the bank was insolvent,” said Al Jazeera’s Latin America editor Lucia Newman.
“The congress right now is tying to impeach the president and the vice president, this session is underway,” she added. “As a I speak, there are people outside urging congress not to accept the resignation of the president because they say that they want him tried and impeached.”
Paraguay’s central bank intervened in ueno after determining that it had breached minimum solvency requirements, setting off a crisis that has left the company’s roughly 3 million customers, in a country of 6.5 million people, unable to access accounts.
“My greatest wish is that the return of those funds be guaranteed, that the deposit guarantee fund fulfill its purpose, and that public funds – as well as the resources that belong to all Paraguayans – be protected,” Pena added in his address.
Ueno has made no public statement on the issue.

articles.title: Was an Italian chef really fired over refusal to put pineapple on pizza?
articles.snippet: The chef had stated that putting pineapple on pizza was "offensive to his culture".
articles.full_text:
Was an Italian chef really fired over refusal to put pineapple on pizza?
Italian chef Davide Tamburella was fired from a Brisbane restaurant in May after the establishment's management expressed concerns about a string of complaints about the chef's behaviour.
Among them were Tamburella's refusal to provide ham and pineapple pizza for guests at a function.
It was the third time Tamburella had refused to use the fruit on pizzas in the past four years.
At the time, the chef had stated that putting pineapple on pizza was "offensive to his culture".
Australia correspondent Katy Watson explains what led to Tamburella's dismissal.

articles.title: The Pitt and ER are similar enough for lawsuit to proceed, judge rules
articles.snippet: The widow of ER creator Michael Crichton argues The Pitt is effectively a reboot of the 1990s series.
articles.full_text:
The Pitt and ER are similar enough for lawsuit to proceed, judge rules
- Published
US drama The Pitt is similar enough to medical series ER for a lawsuit against its producers to progress, a court in the US has ruled.
The widow of Michael Crichton, who created ER, argues The Pitt is effectively a reboot of the series, which has been made without proper permission or credit.
Sherri Crichton says her husband's contract included a "frozen rights" provision that prohibited any spin-offs, sequels or reboots of ER being made without his express consent.
A three-judge panel said there are "clear and numerous similarities between The Pitt and ER," which means the case can go ahead. Warner Bros previously described the lawsuit as "baseless" and sought to have it dismissed.
Listing the similarities between the two shows, the court cited the emergency room setting, the fast pace, use of medical jargon, graphic depictions of injuries, and younger doctors fresh from medical school being trained.
"We find the details here suffice for a prima facie case," the judges said.
It means the case will now go to a jury trial in Los Angeles Superior Court.
But the judges dismissed separate claims against actor-producer Noah Wyle, executive producer John Wells and showrunner R Scott Gemmill.
The justices said there was insufficient evidence to show the three producers were aware they could be violating Crichton's contractual rights.
ER launched in 1994, based on original screenplay written by Crichton. It starred George Clooney, Anthony Edwards, Eriq La Salle and Maria Bello, and aired 331 episodes over the next 15 years.
The show, which followed a group of doctors working in an emergency room in Chicago, was a hit with viewers and critics, and won 23 Emmy Awards during its run including outstanding drama series.
Discussions about a possible reboot of the show began in 2020, and studio Warner Bros spent months negotiating with Crichton's estate.
Those talks were reported to have collapsed over credit and financial guarantees, and producers began developing The Pitt in its place.
But Sherri Crichton and the John Michael Crichton Trust argue the show is a rebranded but uncredited reboot of ER, using the same formula, pacing, style and setting, rather than an entirely original series.
They said producers "simply moved the show from Chicago to Pittsburgh, rebranded it The Pitt, and ploughed ahead without any attribution or compensation for Crichton and his heirs".
Many actors and creatives from ER also work on The Pitt, including Wyle, Gemmill and Wells.
After legal action began in 2024, Warner Bros Television said in a statement that the lawsuit was "baseless", arguing that The Pitt was a "new and original show", adding that the studio would "vigorously defend against these meritless claims".
But in a 33-page opinion published on Wednesday, a three-judge panel unanimously upheld an earlier ruling that Crichton's estate had presented enough evidence to pursue its claim.
Warner Bros had sought to have the lawsuit dismissed on appeal, arguing the shows shared only "generic similarities" common to "any dramatic story involving emergency room doctors".
The judges said they had compared the opening episode scripts for the two shows and found sufficient similarities in plot, themes, dialogue, mood, setting, pace, characters, graphic injury detail and sequence of events.
Sherri Crichton said: "I am deeply gratified by the Court of Appeal decision and look forward to discovery and to our case, which affects writers, creators, and their families and estates, being presented to a jury."
Warner Bros has not yet commented on the latest ruling.

articles.title: Russell Brand is being investigated over two new rape complaints, police say
articles.snippet: Det Supt Andy Furphy said he hoped other potential victims would gain "courage" and "confidence" from the guilty verdicts.
articles.full_text:
Russell Brand is being investigated over two new rape complaints, police say
- Published
Warning: Details of rape and sexual assault
Russell Brand is being investigated over rape allegations made by two more women, it can now be reported.
The disgraced comedian has been found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault by a jury of eight men and four women at Southwark Crown Court, following a three-week trial.
More victims are likely to come forward following his conviction, the detective who led the police investigation has said.
Det Supt Andy Furphy, from the Metropolitan Police, said he hoped other women would gain "courage" and "confidence" from the guilty verdicts.
Brand was found not guilty of two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.
'Ruthless'
Brand had initially been coy and quiet in police interviews, said Furphy, but became bolder as officers continued to question him.
"As he gets used to something, he becomes more emboldened by it," Furphy said. "You can certainly see that in his offending."
Hundreds of people were interviewed as part of the investigation and officers said several witnesses came forward, some of whom had previously had a sexual relationship with Brand. Katy Perry, the US singer who was married to Brand from 2010 to 2012, was not interviewed.
Brand, 51, who was described in court as "ruthless" and a "sexual predator", was once one of the UK's most high-profile and in-demand entertainers.
Some of the women said they had been left "haunted for years" by what he did to them.
Speaking to the BBC, officers working on the three-year Metropolitan Police investigation described how bringing Brand to justice was not without its challenges.
Allegations about Brand's behaviour first emerged in the media in September 2023.
The Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches programme jointly reported that four women had accused him of rape, sexual assault and emotional abuse - claims he strongly denied.
The investigation into other reports against Brand began soon after the story broke.
"We kind of assumed that people might want to come forward," Furphy said, "and people came forward."
Victim reports were made to forces across the country and the Met set up a dedicated team of officers to lead the investigation, which it called Operation Actinolite. Officers said they have since taken more than 340 witness statements - including from Brand's former employers, his ex-colleagues and associates.
One officer was assigned to read Brand's books, watch his stand-up routines and DVDs and listen to his podcasts to help build the case.
Brand's high profile and the intense media scrutiny around him proved a challenge to officers, said Furphy.
Another complexity for the team was the allegations were all "non-recent". The earliest dated back 27 years. It meant there was no CCTV and no forensic evidence to work with.
Furphy said police had to look for other ways to build their case.
"Can we look at where the victims were at the time? Who did they speak to in the aftermath of it? Did they tell anybody else? What other available material is there for us to review that might lend some weight to it? Just because it's non-recent doesn't mean that we can't solve it at all."
A former friend of Brand's was called to court to give evidence for the prosecution, while a statement from the parents of one of the women was heard.
The entertainer's former personal assistant, who worked closely with Brand, told the jury about his "insane sexual appetite".
'Deeply uncomfortable' process
Two months after the police investigation began, Brand was interviewed under caution for the first time. He was interviewed on two further occasions in the following months.
In each interview he provided officers with a prepared statement, which said he did not recognise the complainants or recall the alleged incidents and that if any sexual activity had taken place, it would have been consensual. He then answered "no comment" to the officers' questions.
Charges were brought against Brand in early April 2025: one count of rape, one count of oral rape, two charges of sexual assault and one allegation of indecent assault. The final charge would later be changed to attempted indecent assault at his trial.
The charges all related to women who had come forward since the initial Channel 4 documentary.
The following month he appeared at Westminster Magistrates' Court, in London. He was swarmed by camera crews, so much so that it took him more than two minutes to walk the short distance to the court door. At a later court hearing he pleaded not guilty to the charges.
Meanwhile, women continued to come forward with more allegations.
In July 2025, Brand was interviewed for a fourth time before being charged with further offences: one count of rape and one count of sexual assault. He also denied those allegations.
And then on 14 October 2026, accompanied by his wife Laura, the actor and comedian entered the glass dock at London's Southwark Crown Court for the start of his trial.
The women each came to court and gave evidence to the jury from behind a screen, with Brand listening from the dock. At times they cried as they gave their evidence.
Furphy believes there may be more women who will now come forward.
"I think it's likely - potentially - that other women will come forward," he said. "They'll probably gain some courage and some confidence from what's happened in the courtroom over the last few weeks."
He credits the women for their bravery during what has been at times a "deeply uncomfortable" process. "They are courageous, determined women and our focus has always been on them, not Russell Brand."

articles.title: Joshua Wong, face of Hong Kong's pro-democracy protests, jailed for 10 years
articles.snippet: Wong, 30, is among hundreds of Hongkongers detained under the controversial national security law.
articles.full_text:
Joshua Wong, face of Hong Kong's pro-democracy protests, jailed for 10 years
- Published
Joshua Wong, once the face of Hong Kong's democracy movement, has been sentenced to 10 years in jail for colluding with foreign forces under the city's sweeping national security law.
Wong is among hundreds of campaigners and ordinary Hongkongers arrested under the law, which was imposed in 2020 following explosive pro-democracy protests against Beijing's growing control.
Critics say the far-reaching law has silenced dissent, but authorities argue that it is needed to maintain stability and deny it has weakened the city's cherished autonomy.
Having already spent the last six years in jail, Wong, who was due to be freed in January, will now spend another decade behind bars.
Silenced and erased, Hong Kong's decade of protest is now a defiant memory
- Published30 November 2024
What a defiant mogul's trial says about Hong Kong
- Published18 December 2023
Wong, who turned 30 last month, has already been imprisoned multiple times for his activism which started when he was in his early teens.
On Thursday, he arrived in court wearing a dark blue long-sleeved shirt, khaki trousers and black-rimmed glasses. He looked slimmer compared to his previous public appearances.
He nodded in greeting towards members of the packed public gallery, and took notes intermittently as the judge read out the reasons for his sentencing.
A crowd had gathered outside the court, with dozens of Hongkongers having queued for hours hoping to get a seat in the public gallery. There was also a heavy police presence.
Wong is already serving time for subversion and was due to be freed early next year when he was handed the latest charges, to which he pleaded guilty in September.
Two months and two days of the 10-year term will be served concurrently with his ongoing sentence, the judge said on Thursday.
Prosecutors said Wong had conspired with other campaigners, including self-exiled activist Nathan Law, to lobby for foreign sanctions and blockades against Beijing.
These activities took place between July and late November 2020, the court heard.
Wong and Law had been co-founders of Demosisto, a now defunct pro-democracy political party.
On Thursday, Hong Kong's chief executive John Lee said Wong and Law were "among the primary culprits responsible for undermining Hong Kong's prosperity and stability".
Their actions "not only severely undermined national sovereignty, security, and development interests, but also directly prejudiced the well-being of the general public and the stability of society," Lee said in a statement issued after the ruling.
Beijing's foreign ministry said China "firmly supports [Hong Kong] in safeguarding national security in accordance with the law". It also called on "relevant parties" to "earnestly respect China's sovereignty and Hong Kong's legal system".
Wong's friend and fellow activist Frances Hui, now based in the US, said she was "heartbroken" and "outraged" by the verdict.
"Today's sentencing is not just about Joshua. It is part of a broader political crackdown that seeks to rewrite a chapter of Hong Kong's history and erase the contributions of an entire generation who believed they could shape the future of their city," she told the BBC.
The UK said the sentencing was "a clear example of how the National Security Law is being used to target individuals for political expression and participation". In a statement shared with the BBC, a UK government spokesperson called for "an immediate end to all unjust prosecutions" of individuals charged under the NSL.
According to the US consulate in Hong Kong, the sentencing showed Beijing "will go to extraordinary lengths to silence those who advocate for fundamental freedoms" in the Chinese territory.
Human Rights Watch described the sentence as "cruel and unjust".
"To keep Hong Kong society subdued, and to reduce the chance of an international outcry, the Hong Kong government appears to have adopted the tactic of stacking charges against influential pro-democracy leaders," said its Asia director Elaine Pearson.
The harshest sentence under the controversial national security law (NSL) thus far has been handed to 78-year-old former media tycoon Jimmy Lai, who was jailed for 20 years, also after having been found guilty of colluding with foreign forces.
Who is Joshua Wong?
Born to IT professional Roger and homemaker Grace in October 1996, Wong was diagnosed with dyslexia as a child, which made him struggle with school.
However, he was quick to challenge established rules and norms when they didn't make sense. In secondary school, he rallied with his classmates to protest against the high prices of canteen lunches on Facebook.
In 2011, Wong, then 14, co-founded the pro-democracy student activist group Scholarism, which quickly grew in size and influence.
The following year, the group rallied more than 100,000 people to protest against Hong Kong's plans to implement mandatory "patriotic education" in schools, forcing the authorities to back down.
By 2014, Wong, who was then at the forefront of a civil disobedience movement known as the "Umbrella Movement", had already become one of the most recognisable faces among Hong Kong's pro-democracy activists.
In 2016, he co-founded Demosisto with Nathan Law and Agnes Chow, activists who are now based overseas.
But he often expressed discomfort at being labelled a "protest leader".
"We have a lot of facilitators in this movement and I'm one of them...âInstead of having a top-down command, we now have a bottom-up command hub," Wong told The Financial Times in November 2019.
Demosisto disbanded in 2020, the year Beijing introduced the NSL in Hong Kong.
Law left for the UK and continued his advocacy abroad, while Wong stayed on in Hong Kong and tried to run for a seat in its legislature â but was barred, with authorities citing his opposition to the NSL as one of the reasons.
Meanwhile, the court cases against Wong were stacking up.
On 23 November 2020, he pleaded guilty to several charges related to his involvement in protests outside the Hong Kong police headquarters in 2019.
Then came the NSL charges. While still in prison in February 2021, Wong was among 47 people charged with "conspiracy to commit subversion". The group became known as the Hong Kong 47 and remains the largest prosecution so far under the NSL.
Wong was still serving his 56-month sentence for the subversion conviction when he was charged with collusion under the NSL last year.
On 22 November 2020, the day before he pleaded guilty to the protest charges, Wong wrote in a post on Instagram addressed to "the people of Hong Kong": "To be honest, I have never had much faith in Hong Kong's politics, but I have every confidence in the people of Hong Kong.
"Even as political power now poses a comprehensive challenge to the resilience of our civil society, I believe the people of Hong Kong will, as always, find a way to see things through."
Additional reporting by Martin Yip

articles.title: Typhoons batter East Asia as El Niño makes Pacific 'burn with fever'
articles.snippet: Even for countries where typhoons are a way of life, the last few months have brought unusually wild weather.
articles.full_text:
Typhoons batter East Asia as El NiÃ±o makes Pacific 'burn with fever'
- Published
Wild weather is a way of life for people living along the coast in the Philippines, Taiwan, China and Japan. But the last few months have been extraordinary.
A wave of intense and, at times, unpredictable storms exacerbated by the El NiÃ±o weather pattern has killed dozens, shuttered major airports and wiped out crops and infrastructure across a swathe of East Asia.
In October, nearly all of Taiwan shut down as a monster storm big enough to engulf the island of 23 million roared towards its north-eastern coast. Equivalent to a category five hurricane, Typhoon Champi's 295km/h (193mph) winds had the power to flatten homes and whip up destructive waves.
Thankfully it did not make landfall in Taiwan, skirting past the island while dousing it in rain. But it had far-reaching impacts: hundreds of flights were cancelled in Hong Kong, Taiwan and Japan. In the Philippines' Batanes archipelago, seaside highways shut as huge waves crashed onto the shore, and in southern Japan's Okinawa islands, power was cut to 15,000 homes.
El NiÃ±o is a naturally occurring climate phenomenon in which warm waters pooling in the eastern Pacific and altered wind patterns drive extreme weather events around the world.
It happens around every two to seven years, lasting for around a year. This year's El NiÃ±o, which the UK Met Office has forecast to be the "strongest in living memory", is likely to last until February or March.
In June, Japan watched two storms - Typhoon Mekkhala and Severe Tropical Storm Higos - race towards its eastern coast simultaneously, forcing one million people to evacuate. In July, Tropical Storm Narra grazed China's southern coast along Guangxi, submerging villages and displacing tens of thousands.
August brought Super Typhoon Dolphin, which churned across the Pacific for 16 days - before slamming into eastern China, triggering heavy floods and dozens of casualties.
Later that month Typhoon Saudel made landfall in three south-eastern Chinese cities over one week, shutting transport networks and forcing thousands to evacuate.
'Burning with fever'
The Pacific Ocean, heated to record levels by El NiÃ±o, is now brimming with typhoon energy, according to the Accumulated Cyclone Energy (ACE) metric which measures the total intensity of a season's storms. This year, the ACE reading for South East and East Asia is forecast to be nearly double the 30-year average.
El NiÃ±o also affects wind patterns and in this case, that means typhoons are tending to form further east than usual. They are also becoming stronger as they remain over warm waters for longer.
The Pacific can be likened to someone "burning with fever", says Ana Liza Solis, head of climatology at the Philippines' national weather bureau. "It can go into convulsions soon," she said at a press briefing in Manila in September.
Forecasts suggest the worst may not be over. Last month, sea surface temperatures in the equatorial Pacific - the area monitored by the Japan Meteorological Agency for its El NiÃ±o predictions - soared to 4C above normal, the highest since records began in 1949. The previous record - 3.6C - was set in December 1997.
China's climate agency has warned of sea surface temperatures continuing to rise over the next three months because of the El NiÃ±o.
Despite typhoon season usually peaking around September to October, this is likely to raise concerns across a region that has already been battered by back-to-back storms.
'Very, very scary' simulations
In August, Typhoon Chan-Hom baffled storm watchers in Japan by crossing the country from east to west, as opposed to the usual south-to-north trajectory. Japan's well-resourced and prepared authorities were able to evacuate people swiftly, but this would be far more challenging in some neighbouring countries.
To get a better picture of how rising temperatures could amplify the risks, Manila-based climatologist Rafaela Jane Delfino and colleagues simulated the effects of warmer conditions on the Philippines' most recent monster storms, including 2013's Super Typhoon Haiyan (Yolanda) which killed more than 6,000 people.
They arrived at what she describes as "very, very scary findings": higher temperatures increased total accumulated rainfall by 26%. It's a devastating prospect in a country where flooding from monsoon rains and some 20 tropical storms per year has emerged as one of the main disaster risks.
In recent years, floods have paralysed entire cities for days, and tired of the annual ordeal, Filipinos have taken to the streets to protest against corruption which they say is gnawing away at millions of dollars from flood-control projects.
Delfino, in an article on the University of the Philippines website, insists leaders and officials must gain a better understanding of climate hazards if communities are to be better prepared.
Preparing for the onslaught
Countries are bracing for the immediate impact. Japan has urged citizens to stockpile food and essentials for the typhoon season, and to secure outdoor furniture that could become deadly projectiles when typhoon winds hit. China has asked local officials to identify vulnerable areas and is upgrading its warning and monitoring systems.
The Philippines and its South East Asian neighbours are preparing for disruptions to food production, especially rice, and have increased support for famers, including the provision of fertilisers.
But what happens in the long term is less clear. The window for governments to act on El NiÃ±o is "closing", the United Nations Development Programme in Asia and the Pacific said recently.
"How severely a community experiences an El NiÃ±o is decided years in advance, by where roads and settlements are built, how water is managed, who is covered by social protection and whether public budgets have room to absorb a shock.
"Every El NiÃ±o tests the resilience we have built; this one should also drive us to build more," it added.

AI stocks plunge after US election, driving down markets
Tech stocks lead US market slide as investors weigh impact of midterm election results on AI industry.
United States markets slid on Thursday, with losses in US chip and data centre-related stocks fuelling pressure on the technology sector following Democrats’ sweeping midterm election wins.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq was down 4.8 percent in midday trading, while the S&P 500 fell 3.6 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average slid 2.8 percent.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items- list 1 of 4US markets rise as Democrats sweep midterm elections
- list 2 of 4How US oil firms profit $130bn from Iran war as household bills surge
- list 3 of 4US petrol prices dip ahead of midterms as voters eye costs
- list 4 of 4Can Democrats stop Iran war, reverse Trump’s tariffs after midterms win?
US markets jumped on Wednesday following the midterm election, with Democrats’ sweeping wins signalling limits on policy shocks from a Congress at odds with the White House. Markets were also reassured by US President Donald Trump’s remarks that he would accept the election results.
Artificial intelligence (AI) stocks – which have driven much of the market’s growth – led the plunge in the tech sector that drove down markets on Thursday.
Of the 45 data centre ballot initiatives around the country, voters backed restrictions on most of them. According to Data Centers on the Ballot, 39 ballot measures to restrict AI were successful, while only one — in North Dakota — voted against restrictions.
UBS analysts estimated that potential construction pauses could put roughly 30 percent of planned US data centre capacity additions in 2028 at risk, according to the Reuters news agency.
“Yesterday, markets rallied on certainty as election results removed a layer of uncertainty. Today, portfolio managers and analysts are digging into the implications and adjusting expectations for potential political resistance to AI infrastructure, particularly at the state and local levels,” Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager of Founders 100 ETF, told Al Jazeera.
“We’re seeing that concern reflected in the selloff across semiconductors and hyperscalers.”
Data centre operators and neocloud companies were slumping, with CoreWeave down over 12 percent and Nebius Group down nearly 17 percent. Semiconductor stocks such as AI market leader Nvidia fell by 8.2 percent, Micron by nearly 14 percent and Intel by 6.8 percent in midday trading.
AI server manufacturer Dell dropped nearly 13 percent.
Other tech giants were also in negative territory, with Amazon falling 2 percent and Facebook and Instagram’s parent company, Meta, down 3.8 percent.
SpaceX also took a big hit, with shares down 9.5 percent, while Tesla, also owned by billionaire Elon Musk, fell over 11 percent, following Musk’s nearly half-billion-dollar midterm election spending spree.
In Texas, where both companies are headquartered, Musk bet against Democratic candidates who ended up winning their races. Musk shelled out $230m to defeat US Senate candidate James Talarico, $5m to back Gina Hinojosa’s opponent in the governor’s race and $500,000 in the lieutenant governor’s race, which Democrat Vikki Goodwin won.
“We will believe a SpaceX/Tesla merger happens but now faces a much tougher regulatory roadmap to get this deal done in 2027 given this new political blue roadmap in DC/Texas,” Dan Ives, managing partner of Yorkville Ives, said in a note on Thursday.
Gold prices hit a two-week high on Thursday. Spot gold, which is usually considered a safe investment in times of economic uncertainty, jumped just over one percent to $4,115 per ounce.
Technology stocks also pulled the European benchmark stock index lower on Thursday as investors assessed the outlook for the sector following a Democratic sweep in the US midterm elections, Reuters reported.
“It’s really a story of a rotation happening from technology to non-technology and from the US to non-US markets as a result of the midterm elections and the very aggressive Democratic sweep,” said Ipek Ozkardeskaya, senior analyst at Swissquote Bank.

The service was held in Navahermosa, a town of about 3,000 people in central Spain, where De Miguel’s parents were reportedly born.
A hearse covered in flowers moved slowly towards the church as dozens of mourners, some carrying candles, walked behind. The town hall declared three days of mourning, with flags at half-staff.
De Miguel, 30, suffered cardiac arrest after colliding with Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono while challenging for a high ball during a second‑division match on Monday. He died in hospital the following day.
Spain coach Luis de la Fuente and Real Madrid President Florentino Perez attended the funeral, with De la Fuente saying the game’s community “stands united” in grief.
Police have opened a routine investigation into possible involuntary manslaughter to assess whether the challenge went beyond normal play.
Tributes have poured in from clubs across Europe, with De Miguel’s death described as a rare and shocking tragedy in professional football.

articles.title: Vance eyes 2028 reset, as Republicans mull pivot after US midterms drubbing
articles.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera
articles.snippet: A Democratic 'blue tsunami' in the US midterms shines a light on emerging distaste for Trump's brand among Republicans.
articles.full_text:
Vance eyes 2028 reset, as Republicans mull pivot after US midterms drubbing
A Democratic ‘blue tsunami’ in the US midterms has shone a light on the emerging distaste for the Trump brand within the Republican Party.
Hours after results confirmed that the Republican Party had lost control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives in the United States Congress in the midterm elections this week, senior Republicans were hand-wringing over what had gone so badly wrong and whether a major course correction would now be required.
As once-Republican strongholds like Texas fell to the enemy, US Vice President JD Vance took to X to declare that the “real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone”.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items- list 1 of 3Democrats won Congress. But can they deliver on their promises?
- list 2 of 3Election deniers lose races for governor in key US swing states
- list 3 of 3What’s delaying the US Senate election results in Mississippi and Alaska?
“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night. If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest,” Vance said.
Former Trump voters had switched sides, he said, over the Iran war and the US ties to Israel.
The elephant in the room was no more.
“I remain hopeful about our country. To the people who are pissed off and want to say, ‘I told you so’: you’re right, you did tell us so. Take that energy into electing Republicans who share your worldview,” he wrote.
A poisoned chalice
Just days after the US and Israel launched strikes across Iran on February 28, Tehran effectively closed the critical Strait of Hormuz, which once transited roughly 25 percent of the world’s seaborne oil trade, triggering a massive spike in oil prices and a major global energy crisis. The price of Brent crude – the global benchmark – hit $120 in March and April and has hovered around $115 in recent weeks.
On Thursday morning, oil prices dropped to $93.82 a barrel on expectations that Republican Party losses would reduce the likelihood of US President Donald Trump renewing strikes on Iran following weeks of speculation.
But as consumers in the US struggle with sky-high petrol and diesel prices – not to mention the soaring cost of food, which has also been impacted by Trump’s trade tariffs – the midterms have forced a leadership rethink as the Trump brand appears increasingly toxic.
While no Republicans have declared their intention to run for the 2028 presidential election, some in the party are believed to be eyeing it now.
Andrew Payne, from the Chatham House think tank, told Al Jazeera that any Republican wanting to take on the 2028 election will now need to “distance themselves from the more unpopular aspects of Trump’s record”. That means the Iran war, the greatest poisoned chalice of them all.
“That, I think, is why Vance came out so clearly in blaming the war. It is evident to those who have been watching closely that he has always been the voice of scepticism behind the scenes, and he now needs to make that difference of opinion clear to the average voter. But doing so will be really hard while Trump is still in office and, presumably, wants to play an active role as kingmaker,” Payne said.
Unpopular, but not as unpopular as Trump
The most obvious pick and frontrunner for the Republican 2028 nomination is currently Vance, who is known to have ambitions to take over from Trump.
Regarded as an anti-US interventionist, Vance, while publicly supporting Trump’s Iran war, has also been privately urging him and others to end the conflict, according to the US news outlet Axios.
Last week, Vance sent a letter to the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, proposing a meeting between US and Iranian officials soon in a bid to prevent further escalation. By contrast, this week Trump said the war would only come to an end “when I want it to”.
This move, coupled with his post on X on Wednesday night, is increasingly being seen as Vance putting as much distance as he can between himself and the war.
Throwing off the Trump touch may be trickier than he thinks, however, according to one Vance ally close to the White House who spoke to Politico on Wednesday. While it is “possible for him [Vance] to modestly differentiate himself” from Trump, the source said, there is no way to completely delink himself.
“He’s still Trump’s vice president. This is still a Trump administration war. They’re still both unpopular. He’s not as unpopular as Trump but he’s unpopular,” the anonymous source said.
Pepper Culpepper, a professor at Oxford University’s Blavatnik School of Government, said Vance’s statement on Iran “puts him in a bind”.
“I think what he’s trying to do is communicate that, ‘I was against the war and and I’m the most credible carrier of the anti-war position without antagonising the person who started the war and the person who still wants the war, Donald Trump.’ And every other candidate, [including] Marco Rubio faces exactly the same challenge,” he said.
According to Tuesday polling from The New York Times on who is ahead in a theoretical Republican presidential primary, Vance is at 40 percent. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio follows at 21 percent, alongside Donald Trump Jr, also at 21 percent.
Rubio has yet to comment on the Republican wipeout. Still, like Vance, he is allied with Trump’s administration, which may make a presidential bid challenging.
Any potential candidate now faces a choice between two routes, Payne said. One is to “re-energise the [Make America Great Again or MAGA] movement, which I expect will be difficult, because Trump did it through sheer force of personality that is hard to replicate”.
“The second route is to keep as much of the base on board as possible while appealing to the traditional conservative groups who have drifted from the party over the past decade, thereby expanding the coalition. If he runs, I would think Marco Rubio has a better shot at doing that,” Payne said.
‘Blue tsunami’
There are other potential candidates to consider.
A former frontrunner for the 2016 presidential election, which saw Trump secure his first administration, Ted Cruz is now Texas’s only statewide Republican lawmaker.
In a post on X after the results, Cruz wrote: “2026 was not simply a blue wave; it was a blue tsunami. It was an a** kicking”.
“Food is too high, gas is too high, diesel is too high, insurance is too high, life is too high. Tariffs have made everything too expensive, and the Iran war has dragged on too long. It should have been brief, decisive, and over,” Cruz wrote.
“Understandably, people were pissed off, and elected Republicans didn’t do enough to address their very real pain. So, what do we do now? We need to listen and respond. We need to champion economic policies that make a real difference in working people’s lives, and we need to deal with the consequences.”
In September, the Wall Street Journal reported that Cruz was testing the waters for the 2028 nomination. But as one of the early cheerleaders for the Iran war, Cruz will struggle to disassociate himself from it, other than to criticise the manner of its execution.
As the blame game continues, the Republican Florida governor, Ron DeSantis, described the results of the midterms as “close to an extinction-level event” for the party.
“If the Republican Party doesn’t have Texas as an anchor, then we are not going to be viable nationally going forward,” he said.
“We’re in a very volatile political era, things shift quickly, and the leaders just got to recognise that.”
DeSantis’s time as governor ends in January after two terms, but speculation has grown about whether he also wants to throw his hat into the ring for the US presidential nomination as the playing field remains wide open.

articles.title: Israeli defense company says this trigger is programmed to shoot drones
articles.snippet: The company says the Arbel electromechanical device will release a cadence of fire optimized for shooting down drones.
articles.full_text:
Thailand’s Ministry of Defence began fielding a new computerized rifle trigger designed to help soldiers shoot down small drones, according to last month’s announcement by the device’s manufacturer, Israel Weapon Industries, or IWI. Company officials consider the deployment a real-world endorsement of the Arbel Anti-Drone System as a potential solution for countering drones on the battlefield.
In an interview with Defense News, Semion Dukhan, IWI’s marketing director, described common counter-drone options such as lasers, high-powered electronics, interceptors and specialized ammunition as “not viable in the long run.” He argued that while these technologies can be effective, they often have limitations involving cost, mobility or ease of use. Arbel’s advantage, he said, is its practicality.
“The Arbel is putting a computer to the trigger mechanism of the weapon, so in the context of an anti-drone rifle, what we do is we put the computer in the lower receiver of a standard AR-15 rifle … and with this computer, we control the trigger mechanism of the weapon,” Dukhan said.
He explained that Arbel functions somewhat like a fully automatic weapon in that depressing and holding the trigger engages the system. “So you as an operator, the first bullet that you will shoot, will be purely mechanical … and from the second bullet onward, the system controls the rate of fire to a specific rate of fire that we analyzed as optimal,” he said.
Dukhan said IWI determined the “optimal” rate by analyzing thousands of test shots. “We came down to the specific figure … to get the most chances to hit this kind of target,” he said, describing a target measuring 10 to 15 inches in diameter and flying at roughly 60 kilometers per hour at ranges of 150 to 200 meters.
When IWI unveiled Arbel in 2024, the company said it was intended to improve marksmanship under stressful conditions. Early promotional videos show an operator depressing and holding the trigger before Arbel releases rounds once the system determines the conditions are right.
Dukhan explained that the original version calculates stability and range before discharging a round, whereas the anti-drone version uses an algorithmically calculated rate of fire. “For the anti-drone, it’s only timing. When you, as a user, use the anti-drone algorithm and put it on the Arbel anti-drone safety position, then it only works on timing,” he said.
He added that the option is more “predictable” than the stability-based version, leaving the operator to focus on aiming and following the target. He argued that Arbel can turn anyone with a rifle into a counter-drone operator.
Before Thailand, approximately 25 other countries had already adopted the Arbel system for improving marksmanship or countering drones, according to IWI.

articles.title: MBDA plans to fly ‘fat’ hypersonic interceptor demonstrator before end-2029
articles.snippet: “So it’s a bit fat, but it’s a Formula 1. It’s hypersonic, truly hypersonic, not just Mach 5," MBDA executive Lionel Mazenq said of the envisioned Hydis interceptor missile for Europe.
articles.full_text:
PARIS — An industry consortium developing a European hypersonic interceptor plans to fly a full-systems demonstrator by the end of 2029, project leader MBDA said in a briefing at the Euronaval maritime-defense exhibition.
The program, named Hydis, is competing with the Hydef program coordinated by Spain’s Sistemas de Misiles to secure €100 million (US$112 million) in European funding for the second development phase of the interceptor. A decision about who will get the financing is due at the end of the month, Lionel Mazenq, MBDA’s vice president for program incubators, said Nov. 4.
While China and Russia have been developing hypersonic glide vehicles for attack, Europe lacks capabilities to intercept them, something Hydis and Hydef seek to address. Both projects received European funding for their initial development, but the European Defence Funds plans to fund only one of the two proposals as part of its 2026 work program.
The Hydis interceptor is designed to address a large number of threats that are “very diverse in terms of behavior,” Mazenq said. “Today nothing is able to intercept this portfolio of threats, absolutely nothing.”
With the final concept selected, the consortium is now undertaking a number of on-the-ground demonstrations to bring technology readiness to level 3 or 4 as part of the first phase of the project, the executive said. The commonly used technology readiness scale spans nine tiers, with the highest level representing a system completely developed and proven to work.
For the second phase, Hydis will expand to 36 industrial and research partners as well as 14 subcontractors, from the current 19 companies involved in the project, according to Mazenq. Companies joining the consortium include Safran, which will provide terminal-guidance sensors, as well as Thales, Saab and Leonardo for capabilities such as communication and data links.
The current three-year phase of Hydis, which runs until May 2027, has received €80 million in European funding, with additional funding of €57 million from the four supporting countries France, Italy, Germany and the Netherlands.
The project will expand to 17 countries for the second phase, with 11 member states contributing a combined €133 million of funding in addition to the European money, MBDA said. Germany is dropping out as a partner country for the second phase of the project, according to the briefing documents.
The companies involved in the project will also provide more than €10 million in combined funding, Mazenq said. The consortium is “working on fallback options” should the European Commission choose Hydef instead, though Mazenq said “we are thinking that we will win.”
The second phase is set to run from mid-2027 to mid-2029, and will include full-scale flight trials, according to Mazenq. At the end of the second phase, Hydis aims for a level of technology readiness between 3 and 6 for all functions, with a full-systems demonstrator “by the end of the decade, so very soon after.”
Production of the interceptor is scheduled to start in the first half of the 2030s, the executive said.
France, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands, Sweden and Poland will provide “massive contributions” to the project, with smaller contributions from other countries, he said.
The MBDA executive presented a design for a four-stage missile, a “multi-stage stratospheric hypersonic interceptor” capable of dealing both with hypersonic threats arriving horizontally at medium altitudes, as well as ballistic missiles that approach with a relatively steep dive, and which must be intercepted “relatively early” in the upper layers of the atmosphere.
The Hydis partner countries as well as the European Commission requested an interceptor that covers both ballistic and hypersonic defense, “which requires, effectively, an additional effort in terms of design,” but brings advantages in terms of being able to stockpile a single missile against multiple threats, Mazenq said.
China is probably the country that is ahead in developing hypersonic weapons, more than Russia, with its DF-17 hypersonic glide vehicle the most advanced in service today, according to Mazenq.
“So being obsessed just by Russia is not the solution to prepare a robust system for defending Europe, not only the European continent, but also our forces deployed around the world,” the executive said.
The big challenge of intercepting hypersonic glide vehicles is their maneuverability at altitudes between 30 and 45 kilometers, which means that a slight turn can change the projected interception point by tens or hundreds of kilometers, according to the MBDA executive.
Predicting the trajectory of hypersonic threats will be key to intercepting them, with artificial intelligence running real-time models as soon as a target is detected to identify the right time and place to intercept, updated throughout the flight of the interceptor as it climbs towards its target, Mazenq said.
“This capability is absolutely essential because if you don’t have it, the pressure on the design of the interceptor is such that it’s impossible to do.”
Target and interceptor encounter velocity can reach 5 kilometers per second, according to Mazenq.
The only equivalent to the European program is the U.S. Glide Phase Interceptor project, which was awarded to Northrop Grumman, Mazenq said. The difference with the European project is that GPI only addresses the hypersonic glider threat, with intermediate-range ballistic missiles handled by exoatmospheric interceptors such as SM-3, according to the MBDA executive.
Hydis is aiming for a “robust design” that can be effective with a limited number of sensors. While the system is designed to be integrated with European space-based missile early-warning capabilities JEWEL and Odin’s Eye, it must also be capable of delivering “a good performance” with only a long-range radar, Mazenq said.
“That’s an additional challenge, but this is absolutely necessary to strengthen the future capability and to make it robust to all the conditions that can be encountered during a conflict.”
Hydis aims for its interceptor to cost less than a third of the unit price of an SM-3 missile, according to Mazenq, who didn’t clarify which version of the U.S. missile when asked. The SM-3 Block 1B missile costs $9.7 million to $12.5 million per intercept, while the price tag for the Block IIA missile is $27.9 million, according to the non-profit Missile Defense Advocacy Alliance.
The Hydis concept is hit-to-kill, and the interceptor builds on technology from existing programs, particularly MBDA’s Aster air-defense missile for flight control, while Italy’s Avio provides high-performance solid rocket motors. The system is designed to defeat a hypersonic threat with a maximum of two interceptors fired, according to Mazenq.
A visual comparison with the Aster B1 NT air-defense missile in the presentation indicated an interceptor that stands around 30% taller, with a length of about 7 meters (23 ft). Mazenq said the missile will be compatible with vertical-launch systems onboard ships, including the Mark 41 vertical-launch cell as well as a future version of Naval Group’s Sylver VLS.
“It’s effectively four-stage with a very high capability of acceleration, because we want to fire it as late as possible, due to the indetermination of the hypersonic threat trajectory,” Mazenq said. “So it’s a bit fat, but it’s a Formula 1. It’s hypersonic, truly hypersonic, not just Mach 5.”

articles.title: Amid Iran conflict, ‘non-hostile’ deaths of 2 US airmen raise overseas toll
articles.snippet: Two U.S. airmen supporting operations against Iran died last week in "non-hostile" incidents, raising the death toll to 23 since the war began.
articles.full_text:
Two unidentified U.S. airmen died last week in “non-hostile” incidents amid the war in Iran, raising the number of American fatalities since the war began to 23.
The two airmen are listed under the “non-hostile” category in the Pentagon’s recently updated Defense Casualty Analysis System, or DCAS, meaning their deaths are not related to direct combat operations. One of the deaths was illness- or injury-related, and the other is listed as “pending,” according to the DCAS.
One airman was an active-duty service member, an Air Force spokesperson told Military Times, while the other was in the Air National Guard.
Although typical Department of Defense policy dictates that the names of deceased service members be released to the public 24 hours after next of kin notifications, the Air Force has yet to announce their identities. The spokesperson declined to comment on why their names have been withheld thus far and if the service has been in contact with their families.
Both airmen were white men and mid- to senior-enlisted personnel in E5 to E9 grades, according to DCAS. One was between 31 and 35, while the other was over 35.
One of the airmen passed away in the U.S. Central Command’s area of responsibility, which spans from Northeast Africa across the Middle East to Central and South Asia, the spokesperson said.
The other airman died in the United States; however, the spokesperson declined to comment on where the second airman was operating out of and how they were transported to the U.S.
CENTCOM referred Military Times to the Air Force when asked for comment.
The airman whose death is listed as “pending” is under investigation currently, the spokesperson said, but did not specify by which department.
Another service member whose death was listed as “pending” in DCAS was an Army captain who suffered a medical incident while aboard a military flight on the way to Saudi Arabia in late September.
DCAS lists both of the airmen’s deaths under the Overseas Operations category, instead of Operation Epic Fury, with a Pentagon official telling Military Times it is because the U.S. deems Epic Fury as concluded. The Overseas Operations lists the start date as July 7, aligned with the continued U.S. pressure campaign against Iran.
Officials have been tight-lipped on the exact date Epic Fury was considered terminated, but a defense official previously specified May 5 to Military Times.
The Pentagon’s classification of the operation as an Overseas Operation category faced criticism from Democratic members of Congress, who accused Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth of trying to hide the casualties.
The Overseas Operation category now includes eight service members: four listed as hostile and four as non-hostile. Combining the two categories together makes for a total of 23 service members who have lost their lives since the war in Iran began on Feb. 28, with the Epic Fury category listing 15.
In total, 866 service members have been wounded in action since the war’s beginning across both categories. That includes 417 under Operation Epic Fury and 449 in Overseas Operations, according to DCAS.

articles.title: Under threat of air strikes, US looks to bolster base infrastructure with 3D printing
articles.snippet: U.S. Air Force officials conceded that troop housing at Middle East bases was "never designed for the threat environment now arriving overhead."
articles.full_text:
With many U.S. bases in the Middle East damaged by Iranian bombardment, the U.S. Air Force wants to develop mobile 3D concrete printers to erect buildings quickly.
“Put bluntly, the Air Force has spent decades building exquisite kill chains while too often housing the airmen who sustain them in tents, trailers, and flat-walled structures that were never designed for the threat environment now arriving overhead,” admitted the Air Force’s Small Business Innovation Research solicitation, which will close in January 2027.
Concrete printing, in which printers deposit layers of material to form structures, is gaining traction in commercial construction. The Air Force already used 3D printing to rebuild hurricane-damaged Tyndall Air Force Base, Florida, in 2023, while a Maryland Air National Guard civil engineer squadron is developing its own mobile concrete printer.
But the new SBIR, which is a direct-to-Phase II project, suggests the Air Force wants 3D construction capability imminently. The goal is to enable “military engineers to rapidly print protective structures using automated or semi-automated construction workflows, reduced skilled labor, and locally available cementitious materials where feasible,” the Air Force said.
While 3D concrete printers exist, the Air Force is concerned that the technology is not yet ready to build structures that can survive bombardment by missiles and drones. Hundreds of U.S. military buildings across eight Middle Eastern countries were damaged by Iranian attacks, according to a September 2026 report by the Department of Defense Office of the Inspector General.
The problem is that “the existing state of the art has not yet fully addressed the combined problem that matters most for combat survivability: printable expeditionary materials, field-executable operator workflows, and structure geometry deliberately optimized to mitigate blast-wave behavior and fragmentation effects,” said the SBIR.
The project will evaluate cement-like materials for qualities such as strength, adhesion and the availability of local components. It will develop new construction geometries “that improve survivability beyond conventional flat-wall construction, including shapes intended to reduce blast reflection, limit pressure amplification, interrupt fragmentation paths, and improve internal occupant protection.”
Ultimately, the Air Force wants a mobile concrete printer that can quickly and consistently erect structures while being operated “in austere conditions by lightly trained military personnel.”
The Air Force foresees “substantial” dual-use applications for the mobile concrete printers, such as critical infrastructure and humanitarian relief. However, the SBIR also notes that commercialization will likely require numerous approvals in areas such as building codes.
The aim is to “transition the capability from ‘we can print something interesting’ to ‘a civil engineer unit can deploy, set up, print, inspect, and use protective infrastructure fast enough to matter,’” the service said.
