articles.title: The Pentagon needs more ammo for the Iran war. Small communities are paying the price.
articles.snippet: From polluted waterways to repeated safety violations, the Army’s aging ammunition factories have left a troubling legacy, The War Horse reports.
articles.full_text:
Editor’s note: This article first appeared on The War Horse, an award-winning nonprofit news organization educating the public on military service. Subscribe to their newsletter.
When Hurricane Helene ripped up the East Coast in the fall of 2024, water from the New River flooded towns and destroyed bridges across parts of West Virginia, North Carolina, and Virginia.
In Radford, Virginia, floodwaters crested at 31 feet. Just downstream, the river surged into the Radford Army Ammunition Plant, tearing through warehouse doors and washing out more than a dozen storage containers with thousands of gallons of toxic chemicals inside.
The Army didn’t warn residents until weeks later about the containers filled with dibutyl phthalate, a key component of rocket propellant that has been linked to cancer and reproductive problems in humans — along with hundreds of gallons of diesel fuel and more than 100,000 pounds of wastewater contaminated with calcium sulfate — that had been washed away in the flood. Officials said later that they assumed the containers would sink to the bottom of the river and floodwaters would dilute any chemical leakage.
At least one container, however, washed up on nearby land, where it was partially drained. Two years later, three remain unaccounted for, according to the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality, which found that more than 1,500 gallons had leaked into the environment.
Radford Army Ammunition Plant had already been cited earlier in 2024 for discharging excessive levels of pollutants into the New River. It faced a similar penalty in 2023. And in 2022, Virginia environmental regulators listed Radford as the state’s top releaser of toxins.
“They’re constantly being cited for putting excessive levels of lead into the water, or other toxic releases into the air, or burning more chemicals than they’re supposed to,” said Alyssa Carpenter, a founder of Citizens for Arsenal Accountability, which advocates for stronger environmental practices at Radford.
Radford is also a critical part of the nation’s munitions supply chain: It is the only domestic producer of certain types of propellant used in artillery and rockets. As the Pentagon moves to replenish its depleted munitions stockpile and increase production, it is relying in part on a network of aging Army ammunition plants like Radford, several of which have long histories of violating environmental and safety regulations.
Advocates say the military has too often treated those risks as secondary to production, leaving workers and nearby communities to absorb the consequences.
“The track record of the Department of Defense agencies is not good,” said Mathy Stanislaus, who helped oversee toxic cleanup efforts at the Environmental Protection Agency during the Obama administration. “It’s always defense. ‘That’s our mission.’ Everything else is secondary.”
Now, advocates worry that pressure to produce more ammunition could intensify the risk to local communities. They argue that the costs of rebuilding America’s arsenal are being borne disproportionately by plant workers and the mostly rural communities surrounding the facilities.
“It’s cheap for the military, but it is very expensive for us, for our entire lives,” Carpenter said. “You can’t increase production without increasing the toxic byproducts that come from that production.”
An Aging Arsenal
As the United States entered World War II, the Army built a network of ammunition plants across the country that became part of Franklin Roosevelt’s “arsenal of democracy.” Many were decommissioned after the war and more closed by the end of the Cold War.
Today, much of the defense industrial base is run by private companies, but the Army still manages a network of specialized arsenals, ammunition plants, and maintenance depots, many of which help manufacture, test, and repair missiles, heavy ordnance, and their components, handling work that ranges from creating raw explosive chemicals and rocket propellant to loading warheads and artillery shells.
The United States military is running low on several critical munitions. A report from the Center for Strategic and International Studies published this summer estimated that U.S. inventory of Patriot interceptor missiles had fallen from more than 2,300 at the start of the Iran War to around 800 by the end of July. Stocks of THAAD interceptors, which shoot down incoming ballistic missiles, had likewise fallen by nearly half, from roughly 450 before the war.
The strain predates the Iran War, however. U.S. inventories of precision-guided weapons and heavy conventional ordnance stockpiles had already been under pressure from decades of post-Cold War factory consolidation and shipments to allies overseas.
Before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the United States produced about 14,000 155 mm artillery shells a month. At times, Ukrainian soldiers were burning through that many rounds in just a few days.
And historically, munitions production has often lost out to other priorities in Pentagon budget fights.
“When you’re putting together a budget, you can’t just ask for everything,” said Carlton Haelig, who works on defense strategy at the Center for a New American Security. “When there need to be cuts to pay for an extra squadron [of fighter jets] purchased, another set of transport aircraft, surface ships, whatever, the place that is often considered for making those cuts is in the munitions portfolio.”
In recent years, however, concern about a potential confrontation with China has pushed the Pentagon to expand munitions production. Last year, the Defense Department established a new council tasked with dramatically increasing production of 14 weapons systems, and it has poured billions of dollars toward accelerating production of 155 mm artillery shells.
Environmental advocates worry that pushing more production through aging Army facilities could worsen existing problems with pollution, worker safety, and transparency.
“Measured by the number of sites where hazardous substances have been released into the environment, the military is far and away the largest polluter in the United States,” said Lenny Siegel, an expert on military contamination who leads the Center for Public Environmental Oversight. “I see the simple issue of math. If you’re releasing X into the environment now, you’re going to release 10X when you multiply your production by 10.”
Justine Barati, a spokesperson for the Army Sustainment Command, which oversees these facilities, disagreed.
“The U.S. Army does not, and will never, compromise the safety of our workforce or our surrounding communities to meet production quotas. Protecting our people and the environment is foundational to national security,” she said. “We cannot sustain warfighter readiness without safe, resilient, and compliant installations.”
Barati pointed to a sweeping $18 billion modernization effort across these facilities, saying the Army’s “highest priority” in the modernization is to improve environmental compliance and workplace safety.
But that project is not scheduled to be completed until 2038, and the Army is already accelerating production at some facilities.
“At the same time, the Ukraine war started to get hot and heavy, and we were given the edict that’s like, ‘hurry up and go fast’,” Maj. Gen. John Reim, head of the joint armaments and ammunitions program executive office, told Breaking Defense last year.
EPA records show that all the Army ammunition plants and arsenals involved in producing, testing, or storing weapon components have been cited or flagged for noncompliance by the EPA or state regulators in the past five years. Four of them have been flagged for “significant noncompliance” by the EPA, designating them severe or chronic violators of environmental law. Many of them have also violated state environmental regulations.
EPA records show Scranton Army Ammunition Plant in Pennsylvania, for instance, which helps forge steel 155 mm shell bodies, was flagged for violating the Clean Water Act and Clean Air Act multiple times during 2024 and 2025. At the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in 2023, regulators found workers improperly detonated explosives in a detonation chamber, among other issues. At Holston Army Ammunition Plant in Kingsport, Tennessee, BAE Systems, which operates the plant, was fined this October by the Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation’s air pollution control division for improper record-keeping and reporting of data.
Federal and state regulators can inspect and penalize these facilities, but the fines are often small compared with the sheer size and resources of the Defense Department. After EPA inspectors found alleged violations at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, in 2024, the EPA fined the Army and plant operator American Ordnance just under $40,000 — compare that with a $53 million Army contract American Ordnance was awarded this year for its work at the plant.
“The biggest problem is that the Department of Defense is effectively self-regulating,” Stanislaus, the former EPA official, said.
“When the rubber hits the road, EPA and state agencies simply do not have the authority to mandate certain activities, everything from preventing harm to doing the cleanup.”
A Whistleblower’s Safety Concerns
The fire that erupted on a July night in Crane, Indiana, burned for 15 hours.
Workers at Crane Army Ammunition Activity, which disposes of old munitions, had been storing mortar rounds outdoors in wooden crates beneath a tarp in the baking sun. Temperatures had climbed into the high 90s for several days.
The rounds contained red phosphorus, which can generate heat and flammable gases as it degrades. On the evening of July 6, 2022, nearly 115,000 pounds of red phosphorus ignited, sending flames and smoke billowing into the sky.
What happened before and after illustrates how difficult it can be to hold these facilities accountable.
Three years earlier, Rick Ward, the newly hired safety chief at Crane Army Ammunition Activity, which is housed at Naval Weapons Station Crane, had concerns with safety at the facility. A safety program for controlling hazardous substances was not fully implemented. Hazardous processes weren’t properly classified. Slings used to move heavy explosives didn’t have current certifications.
Ward pointed to an earlier explosion at Crane, in 2013, that sent five people to the hospital. An OSHA inspection afterward identified three dozen safety violations, and an Army “lessons learned” report cited a lack of clear safety procedures.
Ward worried that the safety culture at Crane hadn’t changed. He began bringing concerns up with his supervisors, according to documents he shared with The War Horse.
“Can you imagine taking over as a safety director and knowing that you’ve been handed 36 OSHA violations that never got corrected?” he said.
The year before Ward arrived, EPA had also cited Naval Weapons Station Crane — the base where Crane Army Ammunition Activity is housed — for improperly storing hazardous waste. But Ward felt his concerns were not being taken seriously. So in 2020, he filed an anonymous complaint with OSHA.
Because of COVID-related restrictions, OSHA asked the Army to investigate the allegations itself. Ironically, Crane leaders assigned Ward to conduct the investigation.
About an hour after Ward submitted his report, he said, he was put on administrative leave. He was fired several months later, according to a statement from his lawyers.
Ward has struggled to find work ever since. Crane barred him from the installation, and the Air Force, where he serves as a reserve officer, revoked his security clearance.
“It’s really hard to get a job when you’ve been on the front page of every newspaper in Indiana,” he said.
Barati, the Army Sustainment Command spokesperson, disputed Ward’s account.
“The Army did not retaliate against Mr. Rick Ward in any form or manner. The Army takes workplace safety very seriously and welcomes safety concern feedback from all our employees,” she said.
Many of Ward’s concerns were later substantiated.
A whistleblower investigation partially or fully upheld five of his eight allegations. Among them: Crane did not maintain an accurate list of locations where hazardous work occurred and lacked a complete safety plan for controlling and handling hazardous substances.
EPA inspections in 2023 and 2024 found additional problems at Naval Weapons Station Crane. Inspectors reported materials were still stored in ways that could create fire risks, hazardous materials lacked proper labeling, open containers held corrosive waste, and hazardous waste was kept onsite for more than three times the legal time limit.
“If you mislabel a particular compound, and you put it into a vessel that cannot handle the corrosiveness of that, then it leaks through that vessel and contaminates the ground,” Stanislaus said. “Terrible things can happen.”
Last fall, EPA notified Naval Weapons Station Crane that it planned to assess nearly $250,000 in penalties for the violations.
That is a significant EPA penalty. But for Crane, it’s barely a line item in the budget.
Toxins in the Air
Not long after Alyssa Carpenter graduated from Virginia Tech in 2017, just a few miles from the Radford Army Ammunition Plant, she had to have her thyroid removed. She was 26, otherwise healthy, and had no family history of thyroid cancer. Doctors told her the gland was covered in suspicious nodules.
Carpenter cannot say for sure what caused her condition. But as a student at Virginia Tech, she had advocated for better environmental controls at the plant, and she worries the chemicals the plant releases into the environment may have played a role in her illness.
For decades, Radford and other military facilities have disposed of old munitions and production waste by burning or detonating them in the open, releasing toxic gases, particulate matter, and volatile organic compounds into the air.
The United States generally banned open burning and open detonation of hazardous waste in 1980 but created an exception for explosive waste that could not safely be treated another way. That exception has allowed the practice to continue at military and civilian munition facilities.
In 2025, 45 years after the ban, 64 public and private facilities across the United States were still allowed to burn or detonate hazardous waste.
Residents around Radford have long raised concerns about thyroid disease in the area, though a 2022 review of cancer-registry data by VPM News, a local NPR station, found mixed evidence of unusually high rates. What is clear is that the plant regularly releases hazardous pollutants into the air. According to EPA data, in 2024, Radford released into the air — along with other chemicals — 19,000 pounds of ammonia, which reacts with the atmosphere to create a fine particulate matter known to cause respiratory distress, and more than 900 pounds of lead compounds or lead, a neurotoxin with no known safe level of human exposure. EPA requires facilities to report lead emissions if they exceed just 100 pounds a year.
Barati, the Army Sustainment Command spokesperson, said that Radford had reduced the amount of waste treated by open burning by more than 50% since 2017. She also pointed to a new energetic waste incinerator under construction at the facility that will ultimately replace the need for open burning. The incinerator, originally scheduled to be completed in 2025, will not be operational until 2027, Barati said.
Open burns are subject to environmental limits, and facilities are supposed to account for wind patterns and other factors to make burns safer. But those safeguards can be difficult to enforce.
At Crane, for instance, EPA inspectors cited the facility in 2023 for conducting burns when its own records showed weather conditions outside permitted limits. (Crane officials told the EPA weather was recorded at a different time of day and that the weather was in parameters when it conducted the burns).
Technology has changed since the U.S. allowed an exception for the open burning or detonation of military munitions in 1980. Many other countries, including Germany and Canada, have banned open burning and open detonation of hazardous waste, and military munitions are disposed of in contained burn chambers or closed incinerators. In 2024, the EPA proposed new rules that would further restrict the practice and push facilities toward safer alternative technologies. But the rulemaking has stalled. An EPA spokesperson told The War Horse that the agency plans to finalize the regulations by the end of this year.
The military has moved away from open-air waste burning in recent years at overseas bases.
For decades, troops stationed in Iraq, Afghanistan, and other countries burned everything from medical waste and plastics to old explosives in open burn pits. Military officials defended the pits as a practical necessity in remote war zones.
Like the residents of some communities near ammunition plants in the U.S., service members at bases with burn pits breathed in toxic air containing particulate matter that irritated their throats and lungs, and heavy metals that accumulated in their tissues. When they came home from deployment, they began developing rare cancers and other diseases.
But as veterans reported respiratory illnesses, cancers, and other health problems after breathing in the smoke, public pressure grew. The military eventually curtailed the use of burn pits overseas, and Congress passed the PACT Act in 2022, expanding VA benefits for millions of veterans exposed to the toxic substances during military service — but there are no such benefits for civilians exposed to domestic burn pits.
For Carpenter, that history shows the military can change when the risks become impossible to ignore.
“If it’s toxic for service members, then it’s going to be toxic for community members as well,” she said.
This article from The War Horse was edited by Paul Szoldra, fact-checked by Jess Rohan, and copy-edited by Mitchell Hansen-Dewar.

articles.title: Saildrone expands its European market reach with manufacturing partner in Norway
articles.snippet: CEO Tom Fidjeland told reporters at the Euronaval trade show here that taking on the work of churning out Surveyors was “technically not difficult,” with a first mold already being readied.
articles.full_text:
PARIS — U.S.-based naval drone maker Saildrone has picked Norwegian naval builder Umoe Mandal to produce the Surveyor multipurpose surveillance craft locally, with an eye on new sales in Northern Europe, company executives said.
The Norwegian shipbuilder, headquartered on the country’s southern tip reaching into the North Sea, specializes in composite structures for the naval sector, including masts for British Type 26 frigates. CEO Tom Fidjeland told reporters at the Euronaval trade show here that taking on the work of churning out Surveyors was “technically not difficult,” with a first mold already being readied.
“Mandal’s role in producing the Surveyor will strengthen Europe’s maritime defense industrial base and support the delivery of sovereign maritime domain awareness capabilities to Northern European navies,” Saildrone said in a statement.
The U.S. company will provide its autonomy suite, navigation, electronics and surveillance technology to be mounted on the Norwegian-built Surveyor bodies, the plan goes.
The Surveyor drone is 20 meters long, powered by a diesel motor and wind — a sail-like structure 13 meters high that also houses the onboard electronics. Saildrone markets the vehicle, which can be left alone cruising the ocean for up to 100 days, as a data collector on adversaries and maritime conditions. Multiple drones can be networked to increase the coverage area, according to the manufacturer.
Saildrone’s lineup also includes the smaller Explorer and Voyager models, as well we the larger Spectre, a weapons-capable version still in development.
The partnership comes as the U.S. company has positioned itself to sell naval drones to European navies keen on policing their territorial waters, including in the Baltic and North seas as well as Arctic locales.
Saildrone’s managing director for Europe, Robert Kleist, cited an alliance of Northern European nations Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway and Sweden, NORDEFCO for short, as a potential business generator for naval drones. The pact entails an acquisition track that could spin out national task orders for unmanned platforms, for which Saildrone would then compete, Kleist said.
Umoe Mandall CEO Fidjeland said his company will build a new production site near its main plant devoted to cranking out Surveyors, with an initial production rate of at least two per month.
In October, Saildrone announced a yearlong maritime surveillance mission involving four Voyager drone for the Swedish Navy. Denmark, which straddles the North and Baltic seas, a key transit route for Russian warships heading to the open Atlantic, has been using the craft since 2025.
Saildrone announced a European headquarters in Copenhagen in August, noting plans for an expanded drone production footprint in Europe. Besides Norway, those entail making Spectre boats in the Netherlands at yacht maker Van Der Valk Shipyard, and Surveyor wings in Poland, Saildrone founder and CEO Richard Jenkins said then.

articles.title: Ukraine eyeing new SpaceX Starshield deal by mid-2027, still no answers about October problems
articles.snippet: “I hope that the contract will be signed,” Ukraine’s Chargé d’Affaires Denys Sienik said, even as Kyiv considers potential alternatives to SpaceX.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — With Ukraine’s Starshield contract up in mid-2027, a senior Ukrainian government official said Kyiv is working to hash out the terms of a new deal with the US while also looking at possible stopgap measures.
“As I speak now, we are in the process of starting” those negotiations with Washington, specifically with leaders inside the Pentagon, Ukraine’s Chargé d’Affaires Denys Sienik told reporters at a Defense Writers Group breakfast today.
“I hope that the contract will be signed, and terms of reference will be negotiated, we will have funding, and we’ll be able to defend ourselves,” he added.
Ukraine has relied on SpaceX’s Starshield — the US military variant of the Starlink satellite network — for drone operations against Russian threats and targets. However, in October Ukrainian officials claimed a sudden change to the Starshield network, which they directly attributed to the failure of drones and defenses that led to military and civilian deaths.
Around this same time, US President Donald Trump announced he had reached a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel to help lower the cost of fuel, while also warning Ukraine not to strike Russian refineries. The confluence of events raised a series of questions about what changed with Starshield: Was it a technical glitch, or did someone inside the US government or SpaceX — specifically CEO Elon Musk — give the order?
“We still don’t have [an] answer from Pentagon and SpaceX [about] what has happened” but it is “working now,” Sienik said.
“Good news is that it has been resolved, and our military can further do their work… Do we want another situation like that? Definitely no,” he added.
Despite Ukraine’s problems with Starshield in October, Sienik said the country needs the new contract to go through since there is “no effective alternative” to the low-Earth orbit satellite system. However, he emphasized that Ukraine is looking around at options, for both the short and long term.
“We are working on our capabilities domestically in Ukraine [and] Europeans are also working on their system,” Sienik added. “Everyone understands that it’s always good to have a backup.”
Sienik’s comments came just days after the US mid-term elections with Democrats poised to reclaim control of the Senate and House. Once in power, they are expected to begin holding new oversight hearings into an array for defense-released topics that may include such topics on Ukraine like Starshield, and the slow rolling of $400 million in military air to the Eastern European nation.
During today’s roundtable, Sienik said Ukrainian officials will answer any questions lawmakers have but do not want to interfere with domestic affairs. However, he reasserted the plea for key US air defense capabilities like Patriot interceptors and additional F-16 fighter jets.
“The issue with the existing F-16s is that they are old, and we overuse them because they are super effective: We don’t have enough of them,” he said.

articles.title: Saildrone inks agreement with Norwegian shipbuilder Umoe Mandal to produce USVs
articles.snippet: The agreement is the latest in a series of moves by Saildrone to expand into Europe.
articles.full_text:
PARIS — Saildrone and Norwegian shipbuilding company Umoe Mandal have signed an agreement to produce unmanned surface vessels, with some parts being built in Norway, company executives said.
Under the agreement, signed Wednesday at the Euronaval defense show here, the Norwegian company will build the vessel for Saildrone’s 20-meter-long Surveyor USV, and the US-based manufacturer will provide the autonomy suite as well as electronics and navigation systems.
“The Saildrone Surveyor will provide persistent maritime domain awareness in strategically important waters, including the Baltic and North Seas, as well as Arctic waters, while giving customers sovereign control over their operations and data,” Robert Kleist, Saildrone’s European managing director, told reporters here.
The representative added that Umoe Mandal was selected for its expertise in composite structures, such as glass or carbon fiber. Among other things, the Norwegian company supplies the mast for the British Type-26 frigates.
The agreement is the latest in a series of moves by Saildrone to expand into Europe. Over the summer, the company opened a new headquarters in Copenhagen and, in August, signed an agreement with Polish company Southern Spars to produce Surveyor’s wings in Poland.
Umoe Mandall CEO Tom Fidgeland told reporters that his company has already begun building a new manufacturing site near its main plant, dedicated to producing the USVs.
“This is to answer the demand we know will come in the future. We are doing this without having concrete orders [yet] in place, but we are confident this will be the case based on future work. … We can easily reach two vessels a month, but that can be expanded more than that for sure,” Fidgeland said.
Kleist cited Northern European countries, including Denmark, Finland, Sweden, and Norway, as anticipated interested parties for Saildrone USVs, which could be facilitated through the Nordic Defence Cooperation (NORDEFCO) framework agreement.
The NORDEFCO agreement allows Nordic nations — Norway, Denmark, Finland and Iceland — to rapidly procure different types of systems, including USVs. It follows a sort of surveillance-as-a-service model: instead of buying physical USVs, member countries can contract Saildrone to deliver maritime intelligence.
In October, the Swedish Armed Forces became the first country to execute a national deployment under the NORDEFCO framework, launching a year-long maritime surveillance mission in the Baltic Sea using 4 four Saildrone-made Voyager USVs. In this context, Saildrone operates the vessels, which sail under the Swedish flag, and the Swedish Navy chooses the mission parameters and receives a continuous stream of data.
Kleist said that if other countries opted to adopt this model, it could benefit the regional allies, as they would essentially be looking at the same information, for instance, surveillance of Baltic Sea activities, and could potentially share intelligence among nations as well.
The Baltic Sea is a key maritime area for Europe, as it connects many shipping routes and critical underwater infrastructure. Some countries have vocalized increased concerns over the protection of such infrastructure, with the rise of hybrid warfare and sabotage incidents seen in Europe in recent months. In addition, Russia has direct access to the Baltic Sea through several entry points: Saint Petersburg and the Leningrad Oblast in the east, as well as through the Kaliningrad exclave — situated between Poland and Lithuania.
When asked whether the companies were worried about Russian forces seizing one of the USVs, Fidgeland said they must consider it, but are not concerned it would happen.
“We have radars, we have cameras… We can see them [Russians] miles away. If they have bad intentions, we can take nice photographs of them,” Fidgeland told Breaking Defense.

articles.title: Fairbanks Morse Defense in talks with Navy about Seawolf-class submarine repairs
articles.snippet: Fairbanks Morse Defense is already conducting repairs on the Ohio- and Los Angeles-class submarines.
articles.full_text:
PARIS — Fairbanks Morse Defense (FMD) is poised to conduct repairs on the US Navy’s three Seawolf-class submarines, as the company expands its submarine maintenance footprint.
FMD’s preparations to repair the submarines come just after US Naval Sea Systems Command awarded the firm an approximately $100 million follow-on contract in October to conduct Emergency Diesel Generator (EDG) overhauls on six aging Los Angeles- and Ohio-class submarines, part of a broader effort to extend the vessels’ service lives by as many as 14 years.
The Seawolf-class submarines, the first of which entered the fleet in 1997, could be next in line for maintenance. Fairbanks Morse Defense CEO George Whittier confirmed that the company is now in discussions with the Navy about conducting maintenance on the Seawolf subs. He expects work on those vessels to begin after the Los Angeles- and Ohio-class submarine overhauls, which are expected to wrap up in the late 2020s.
“We’re going to end up doing overhauls on those as well, right?” Whittier told Breaking Defense at the Euronaval defense exposition in Paris about the Seawolf class. “Because again, they’re 25, 30-year-old boats, right? So all of that’s going to be coming.”
Submarine maintenance delays have perpetually been a thorny issue for the Navy. For example, the Government Accountability Office issued a report in August that found public shipyards, which perform maintenance on nuclear-powered vessels like submarines, completed only 11 percent of submarine maintenance periods on schedule.
Additionally, the Navy is facing questions about whether it can deliver the Columbia-class submarine by a 2028 target. As a result, the new contract to extend the lives of the Los Angeles- and Ohio-class submarines tackles “the geopolitical risk of a post-2029 submarine deficit” stemming from potential delays in Columbia-class and Virginia-class submarine construction, as well as the decommissioning of other aging vessels, FMD said in a news release in October.
The October contract builds upon a previous NAVSEA award under which FMD completed emergency diesel generator overhauls on two Ohio-class submarines, and one Los Angeles-class submarine.
Keith Haasl, FMD president of Services and Technology, said in an October statement, that the contract reflects growing investment in submarine capabilities by the United States and its allies, as well as by competitors Russia and China, which are expanding and modernizing their own fleets.
“Because the timely delivery of critical components dictates fleet availability, we are moving quickly to scale our capabilities,” Haasl said. “Our work with the Navy actively demonstrates principles of rapid submarine maintenance and overhaul that we can share with allies, so we can ensure operationally ready submarines faster.”
FMD is also looking to accelerate its Pit Stop maintenance program, an initiative inspired by NASCAR and Formula One that uses pre-staged original equipment manufacturer parts, standardized procedures and the company’s robotic welding platform to reduce repair timelines.
The company has completed roughly 10 Pit Stops with the Navy over the past five years, and is targeting another 10 in 2027, Whittier said. Those 10 planned Pit Stops next year will cover surface ships.
Separately, FMD also announced in October that it has begun expanding its subsidiary facility, the Bird-Johnson Propeller Company in Pascagoula, Miss., in an effort to double its naval propulsion system capacity. The expansion includes a $27 million investment from the Navy — funded largely through Australia’s US Submarine Industrial Base contribution as part of the AUKUS Pillar I agreement.

articles.title: Shield AI acquires radar firm Echodyne in $5.3B deal
articles.snippet: The deal, which is expected to close in early 2027, will give Shield an in-house counter-UAS offering
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — Defense tech firm Shield AI is acquiring Echodyne, a provider of counter-drone radar systems, in a $5.3 billion deal, the companies announced today.
The deal, which is expected to close in early 2027, will give Shield an in-house counter-UAS offering, according to a company statement. Echodyne says its counter-drone systems are “used by defense, government and commercial customers in more than 40 countries.” Further, its Metamaterials Electronically Scanned Array (MESA) system was selected in September by the Pentagon’s Joint Interagency Task Force 401 to supply counter-drone systems to the US military.
The addition of a counter-drone radar system is an interesting add to Shield, which has several different product lines, ranging from autonomy software that has been used on multiple Pentagon projects, to the large X-Bat drone the company now hopes to market globally.
Shield has a history of product expansion through acquisition. It’s V-Bat drone, and hence the push for X-Bat, came form a 2021 acquisition of Martin UAV. And earlier this year, the firm closed on the purchase of Aechelon Technologies, a simulation software firm.
“The acquisition of Echodyne dramatically accelerates our efforts to meet growing customer demand for multi-mission capabilities, provides increased access to a rapidly expanding counter-drone industry, and further diversifies our revenue streams with sustained, compelling growth for the combined company,” Shield CEO Gary Steele said in a statement, noting the company structure now consists of three buckets: autonomy software, autonomous systems and mission systems.
“Hundreds of customers rely on our radars to detect and track drones, protect people and infrastructure, secure borders, and ensure safe airspace operations. Shield shares our view that autonomous systems can only act on what they can sense, and superior sensors lead to superior systems and outcomes,” Echodyne CEO Eben Frankenberg added. “By joining Shield, we’re creating a company with the size and breadth to deliver even more value to our broad range of defense, government, and commercial customers around the globe.”
Echodyne will operate as a business unit within Shield’s mission systems business, with Frankenberg staying on and reporting up to Steele as part of the company’s executive team. There are no planned workforce reductions, and Echodyne employees will not be required to relocate, according to a Shield spokesperson. Longer term, there will likely be greater integration of Echodyne products across Shield’s portfolio.
While the company is not announcing any “specific aircraft integrations” right now, the spokesperson noted that “Autonomous systems can only act on what they can sense, and Shield expects autonomous aircraft to need more capable onboard sensors in the coming years. Echodyne’s radar is built for that use. The acquisition also adds radar engineering, manufacturing capacity and a commercial customer base to Shield’s business.”
The spokesperson added that the Echodyne deal has no impact on the recent decision to work with RTX for a radar on X-Bat, saying that work “is separate from this acquisition.”
Of the $5.3 billion deal, $4.8 billion will be paid out at closing with another $500 million paid out upon Echodyne meeting spelled out performance targets. Coinciding with the deal, Shield raised $2.5 billion through Series H funding and investments from Blackstone and JPMorgan Chase.
The spokesperson also noted that the company “will continue to look at acquisitions as part of its growth strategy.”

articles.title: Eurofighter eyes sales of 200 additional aircraft
articles.snippet: Potential new deals include second batch orders for Turkey and the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, jointly amounting to 78 units, while closing an order from Austria would add a further 36 aircraft.
articles.full_text:
MUNICH — The Eurofighter consortium is eyeing global market “opportunities” to sell more than 200 of the multirole fighter jets, an infographic shared by the consortium during the International Fighter Conference showed.
Potential new deals of the combat aircraft include second batch orders for Turkey and the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, jointly amounting to 78 units, while closing an order from Austria would add a further 36 aircraft.
A breakdown of customers and associated aircraft quantities representing 86 or more aircraft from the 200-plus projection was not shared, but the consortium has long expressed interest in exporting to countries like Portugal, Poland and Bangladesh.
Portugal is in need of replacing a fleet of aging F-16 fighter jets, with a successor solution pitting Eurofighter, Lockheed Martin’s F-35, Sweden’s Gripen and France’s Rafale against one another. Airbus is leading the Eurofighter consortium’s sales campaign with Lisbon.
“Our proposal offering the Eurofighter Typhoon to replace Portugal’s F-16 fleet is currently in its final stages of preparation,” an Airbus spokesperson told Breaking Defense in a statement today. “To capture the full spectrum of operational sovereignty, life-cycle value, and industrial collaboration opportunities for the Portuguese Government and national industry, the comprehensive proposal will be formally submitted by the end of this year.”
Similarly, Warsaw is eyeing a contract to acquire 32 additional fighter jets in support of an air superiority program requirement. However, it could decide to procure more US F-35 fighter jets after securing a $4 billion Foreign Military Financing (FMF) loan from Washington in September.
Last year, Italy’s Leonardo and the Bangladesh air force signed a letter of intent aimed at opening talks on a Eurofighter deal with Bangladesh, but Dhaka has also moved toward negotiating with China over an acquisition of rival J-10CE fighter jets, according Reuters report.
The number of potential exports for Eurofighter has increased from last year’s figure of 134 units, shared at the 2025 edition of the International Fighter Conference. At the time, Eurofighter CEO Tamarit Degenhardt told Breaking Defense that Turkey’s initial order for the multirole combat jet could serve as a “wake-up call” for other nations to ink new deals.
In 2025, Turkey signed a $10.7 billion deal with the UK for the acquisition of 20 Typhoons, solidifying a prior MoU between the two nations for a total of 40 aircraft.
As for current manufacturing developments, additional figures shared this week at the conference indicate that 60 aircraft are currently in production as the consortium executes contracts with Spain, Germany and Kuwait.
Recent orders including the Turkish deal, amount to 89 aircraft set for future production and in line with acquisitions from Spain (Halcon 2), Germany (Tranche 5) and Italy.
No update was provided relating to plans for a production ramp up, but Degenhardt noted last year that he is targeting a rate of 30 aircraft a year beginning in 2028 — based on securing new export business.

WASHINGTON — Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao has appointed Rear Adm. Jonathan Rucker to lead Portfolio Acquisition Executive Maritime, the service announced today.
“President [Donald] Trump has given me a clear mandate: build the Golden Fleet,” Cao said in a statement from the Navy. “Admiral Rucker is the right leader at the right time to bring accountability to and accelerate our American shipbuilding system.”
As PAE Maritime, Rucker will lead “the Navy’s surface ship acquisition efforts across the shipbuilding enterprise.”
“We owe it to our Sailors and Marines to deliver the ships they need at speed with capability and quality to ensure they maintain our competitive advantage,” Rucker said in the statement. “I am eager to build the Fleet America needs now.”
PAE Maritime was one of five PAE organizations stood up by the Navy in March as part of a wider acquisition reform initiative across the services. The office oversees acquisition programs for the entire surface fleet, including carriers, combatants and auxiliary vessels.
Among its notable programs is the service’s Medium Landing Ship (LSM) program, which last week awarded Hanwha Defense USA the right to construct a new vessel in a $269 million deal
Before today, Rucker served as a director of design and construction for Direct Reporting Portfolio Manager (DRPM) Submarines beginning in April. Prior to that, he was the Program Executive Officer (PEO) for Attack Submarines, according to the announcement.
Rucker takes over for Chris Miller, who served as the inaugural chief of PAE Maritime. On Oct. 13, Cao formally appointed Miller to serve as both the PAE and DRPM for Robotic and Autonomous Systems (RAS) concurrently, according to a statement from the Navy.

articles.title: Russian state-linked hackers target iPhone, Android devices in zero-click espionage campaign
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Russian state-linked hackers targeted users in Ukraine, the United States and Europe in a campaign to steal sensitive information from iPhone and Android devices, researchers found.
articles.full_text:
Russian state-linked hackers target iPhone, Android devices in zero-click espionage campaign
Russian state-linked hackers targeted users in Ukraine, the United States and Europe in a campaign designed to steal sensitive information from iPhones and Android devices, researchers found.
French cybersecurity firm Sekoia attributed the operation to APT29, also known as Cozy Bear or Midnight Blizzard, an espionage group widely believed to operate on behalf of Russia's foreign intelligence service (SVR).
To reach potential victims, the hackers planted malicious code on legitimate websites, created fake versions of popular websites and compromised a Ukrainian web analytics service, researchers said in a report on Wednesday.
The attackers were able to steal passwords, messages, emails, browser data and other sensitive information from vulnerable devices, in some cases without requiring users to click on anything or download malicious files.
The investigation began after researchers discovered malicious code on the website of an unnamed Ukrainian gas production company. Further analysis uncovered similar compromises affecting other organizations, including a major U.S. chemical industry trade association and a far-right European political party.
The hackers also created fake versions of two high-profile websites: America250, an initiative commemorating the 250th anniversary of U.S. independence, and Raffles London at The OWO, a luxury hotel near several British government buildings.
The fraudulent websites displayed content from the legitimate sites they were spoofing while also running malicious code designed to identify visitors using vulnerable devices.
Researchers suggested that the fake America250 website could have been used to lure victims with invitations to anniversary events, while the hotel website may have been intended to target diplomats and other high-profile guests. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky reportedly stayed at the Raffles in London during an October visit, although researchers found no evidence that he was targeted.
In one of the campaign's most far-reaching operations, the attackers compromised Plerdy, a Ukrainian web analytics service used by thousands of websites, most of them based in Ukraine.
Between late August and early September, the hackers inserted malicious code into a tracking script distributed through the service, potentially exposing visitors who browsed hundreds of websites, including those associated with the Ukrainian military, special forces and manufacturers of drones and other military equipment.
The compromised script allowed the attackers to identify visitors' devices and software versions before attempting to exploit known security flaws.
Sekoia said it was unclear whether the hackers were targeting specific individuals or attempting to collect information from as many vulnerable devices as possible before identifying valuable targets.
Stealing smartphone data
The hackers used different attack methods depending on the device and operating system.
On older iPhones running iOS 16, the attacks sought to steal browser and application cookies, which could potentially allow hackers to access online accounts. A more advanced attack targeting vulnerable iPhones running iOS 18.5 could extract messages, emails, passwords, contacts, photos and location history, as well as information stored by messaging apps, including WhatsApp and Telegram.
That attack relied on a toolkit known as DarkSword, a suspected commercially developed surveillance tool capable of extracting large amounts of information from iPhones. DarkSword has previously been used by other threat actors in operations targeting users in Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Malaysia.
On Android devices, the hackers exploited vulnerabilities in older versions of Google's Chrome browser to steal browsing data, cookies and saved Wi-Fi passwords.
Unlike some spyware operations, the attacks were designed to extract information without maintaining long-term access to compromised devices.
All three attack methods relied on previously discovered vulnerabilities that Apple and Google had already patched before the campaign began. Researchers said the attacks did not exploit previously unknown software flaws, known as zero-days, and would not work against fully updated devices.
Sekoia did not establish how many smartphones were successfully compromised or how much information the hackers obtained. The company said it was working with computer emergency response teams in affected countries to identify potential victims and explore ways to disrupt the hackers' infrastructure.

articles.title: Chainalysis warns all users hit in cyber breach involving ‘agentic’ techniques
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Chainalysis, the blockchain analytics company, said Wednesday night that some information belonging to all its users — which its website says include those in the law enforcement and national security sectors — had been exposed in a cyberattack.
articles.full_text:
Chainalysis warns all users hit in cyber breach involving ‘agentic’ techniques
Chainalysis, the blockchain analytics company, said Wednesday night that some information belonging to all its users — which its website says include those in the law enforcement and national security sectors — had been exposed in a cyberattack.
The company initially disclosed a breach on October 30, although at the time said it had found no evidence that authentication credentials or session tokens had been accessed.
In its latest update, posted Wednesday night, the company said it had discovered “certain customer information including names, usernames, password hashes and live tokens for all Chainalysis users were exposed to a malicious actor.”
The perpetrator was not identified. Chainalysis previously said it had “detected an external actor using offensive agentic techniques to gain unauthorized access to Chainalysis systems and internal tools.” It has not explained what it meant by “offensive agentic techniques.”
The company initially told customers the breach came amid what it described as “an industry-wide rise in AI-driven cyberattacks.” Although it initially mentioned agentic techniques, it did not explicitly say its own breach was caused by an AI agent.
Chainalysis said it had engaged “world-class third-party cybersecurity experts” to help investigate the incident and strengthen its defenses.
Its statement did not specify whether every category of information was exposed for every user, nor did it say how many users it has.
According to its website, Chainalysis says it provides services to more than 1,500 customers across sectors including law enforcement, cryptocurrency and regular finance, regulators and national security.
“At this time we continue to have no evidence that any investigations data has been accessed or Chainalysis attribution data has been manipulated,” the company said Wednesday night.
All users will have to reset their passwords and rotate API keys as appropriate, the company said, also urging affected customers to visit its login page directly rather than follow links in password-reset emails.
Chainalysis did not explain what it meant by “live tokens” nor say how the exposed passwords had been hashed. Certain password hashes can be cracked to recover the original password, while active authentication tokens may allow attackers to access accounts without passwords.
The company also said Wednesday night that some customers' accounts on its Know Your Transaction service (KYT) — used to monitor cryptocurrency transactions for suspicious activity — appeared to have been accessed.
The suspected account access was disclosed amid widening disruption to the company’s services as Chainalysis provided updates on its ongoing investigation.
The company said some customers’ passwords had been exposed in an “on-path attack,” in which an attacker intercepts communications between users and a service.
An email to affected customers described an “ongoing multifront cyberattack” but did not identify the other fronts. It said the interception method had been contained and remediated, affected accounts were being locked and there was no evidence they had been accessed improperly.
Forty minutes later, Chainalysis said “abnormal activity” had prompted it to take KYT's user interface and API, other address-screening products and its login page offline.
Customers who had just been instructed to reset their passwords were told doing so was not immediately possible.
The shutdown expanded restrictions imposed Monday, when the company took its Reactor investigations tool and Data Solutions product offline as a precaution but kept its compliance transaction-monitoring products running. Chainalysis describes those products as important to detecting money laundering across the cryptocurrency ecosystem.
The company said it planned to begin restoring KYT and Address Screening on Thursday, after customers submitted trusted IP addresses to be added to an allowlist. Customers would then be able to reset passwords and rotate API keys.
It gave no date for restoring Reactor, Data Solutions or another product, Chain (Beta), and did not explain how customers were screening transactions while KYT was offline.
Chainalysis has also not said whether the password interception, exposure of hashes and tokens, and suspected unauthorized account access involved the same attacker or methods.
A spokesperson said they were unable to share more information than was provided in the blog.

articles.title: Ukraine fires two senior security officials amid corruption probe into scam call centers
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Ukraine's security service has fired two senior officials amid a corruption investigation into an alleged criminal network that bribed law enforcement officers to protect fraudulent call centers and other illegal operations.
articles.full_text:
Ukraine fires two senior security officials amid corruption probe into scam call centers
Ukraine's security service has fired two senior officials amid a corruption investigation into an alleged criminal network that bribed law enforcement officers to protect fraudulent call centers and other illegal operations.
The dismissals, announced Wednesday evening by Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) chief Oleksandr Poklad, came as anti-corruption investigators searched properties linked to several senior security officials.
The National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO) said earlier Wednesday that they had uncovered a criminal organization that paid bribes to senior officials in exchange for allowing scam call centers to operate without interference.
The investigation, dubbed Operation Carthage, is part of a broader crackdown on fraudulent call centers that have operated in Ukraine under the protection of local authorities.
The alleged network included at least 12 people, among them senior officials from the SBU, the Prosecutor General's Office and the National Police, as well as individuals linked to organized crime.
According to investigators, the group's activities extended beyond online fraud to drug trafficking, counterfeit cigarette production and currency forgery. Its members also allegedly organized kidnappings, assaults and other acts of violence.
"The criminal organization used corrupt connections within law enforcement agencies to protect its illegal activities and generate illicit profits," NABU said.
Poklad did not identify the two dismissed officials but said the SBU was cooperating fully with investigators.
"The Security Service expects a transparent, objective and impartial investigation," Poklad said in a statement. He added that he was in contact with intelligence agencies in partner countries to ensure that suspected crimes were also investigated abroad.
NABU said detectives encountered resistance during one court-authorized search when a senior SBU official threatened to use a firearm and prevented investigators from entering the premises.
The latest allegations follow an earlier investigation disclosed in September into a suspected bribery scheme involving officials in the office of then-Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko.
Investigators alleged that officials had collected payments from fraudulent call centers since mid-2025 in exchange for ensuring that police and prosecutors did not interfere with their operations. The centers allegedly targeted victims both in Ukraine and abroad.
Kravchenko denied involvement in protecting the operations and subsequently submitted his resignation. He later left Ukraine, saying he was traveling on official business.
The scandal has also prompted lawmakers to strengthen penalties for online fraud.
In mid-September, Ukraine's parliament approved legislation introducing specific criminal penalties for establishing, operating or working at fraudulent call centers, as well as recruiting people to participate in such schemes.
The legislation also targeted fraud carried out through electronic communications, including the misuse of stolen personal and banking information. Those convicted of involvement in fraudulent call centers could face prison sentences of seven to 12 years under the new legislation.
Fraudulent call centers have become a persistent problem in Ukraine, with criminal groups employing teams of operators to trick victims into transferring money or providing access to their bank accounts.
According to Ukraine's National Police, scammers frequently impersonate bank employees, law enforcement officers or financial advisers. Some lure victims onto fraudulent investment platforms, while others spoof phone numbers to make calls appear to come from legitimate institutions.

articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Japan Airlines, Cathay Pacific, Korean Air, Asiana Airlines, Singapore Airlines and Malaysia Airlines have all come forward over the last week to report data breaches traced back to Amadeus IT Group — a company that builds and maintains platforms for flight reservation, ticketing and check-in platforms.
articles.full_text:
More Asian airlines announce data breaches after attack on Spanish IT provider Amadeus
Multiple airlines in Asia are reporting data breaches after a cyberattack on a Spanish IT provider exposed customer details.
Japan Airlines, Cathay Pacific, Korean Air, Asiana Airlines, Singapore Airlines and Malaysia Airlines have all come forward over the last week to report data breaches traced back to Amadeus IT Group — a company that builds and maintains platforms for flight reservation, ticketing and check-in platforms.
A spokesperson for Amadeus told Recorded Future News that it recently became aware of a vulnerability affecting a travel booking display environment.
“Certain booking-display data was accessible through the vulnerability. Although our investigations continue, we can confirm that there is no evidence that payment or financial data was accessed,” the spokesperson said. “There are no indications that this vulnerability has been exploited for ransomware purposes. Amadeus implemented measures to fix the vulnerability as well as enhanced monitoring and detection capabilities. We are in direct dialogue with our customers and authorities.”
The company declined to say whether the attackers have contacted them or how many total victims were impacted by the attack.
Japan Airlines said 92,000 customers had information stolen and Singapore Airlines said 46,000 records were accessed. Cathay Pacific said 53,000 records were stolen by the hackers, including booking numbers, passenger names and flight details. Some records included passports and other travel documents as well as frequent flyer numbers and email addresses.
The company said they were told by Amadeus that the threat actors used “login credentials assigned to its system account” during the breach but did not explain the incident further. Singapore Airlines told Reuters and Bloomberg that confirmation numbers, travel itineraries and names were leaked as part of the incident.
Singapore Airlines said it would contact people with upcoming flights to change their now-exposed booking numbers and urged customers to be wary of malicious emails.
All the airlines said the cyberattack on Amadeus did not impact their own systems or operations.
Amadeus reported more than $6.5 billion in revenue last year and has deals with hundreds of airlines and airports for IT services and technology platforms for ticketing and reservations.
Dozens of airlines have been attacked by cybercriminals over the last year, including incidents in 2026 involving Spanish airline Iberia and Air Côte d'Ivoire. Hacker stole 6 million customer records last year from Australian airline Qantas in an incident that eventually led to the company’s senior executives being fined hundreds of thousands of dollars.

articles.title: Canadian extradited to US for allegedly hacking schools in at least four states
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: The Department of Justice said it identified two suspects in a case that dates back to 2016 and involved illicit cryptomining on the computers of U.S. educational institutions.
articles.full_text:
Canadian extradited to US for allegedly hacking schools in at least four states
The Department of Justice indicted two Canadian nationals, with one already in the U.S. to face charges, for allegedly running a hacking campaign in 2016 that targeted educational institutions in multiple states.
Ryan James Roach, 35, and Mathiew James Stubbings, 41, are accused of hacking into computers, stealing login credentials and using compromised devices to mine cryptocurrency. Stubbings and Roach started the campaign in June 2016 and continued until December 2019.
Roach was arrested and extradited from Canada last week. He appeared in a Rochester, New York, federal court on Tuesday.
The Justice Department said it is still trying to secure Stubbings’ extradition in Canadian court.
Both men are facing a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison on charges of conspiracy to obtain information from a protected computer and to cause damage to a protected computer, obtaining information from a protected computer, and intentional damage to a protected computer.
The two were able to conduct the attacks by using virtual private servers in several European countries, according to prosecutors. They hacked into educational institutions in New York, Tennessee, North Carolina, and Massachusetts before installing cryptomining software on computers.
Prosecutors said they targeted “educational institutions in the United States that had supercomputers and researched security vulnerabilities in the victim computer networks, using a variety of methods to gain access, including using a server and compromised computers from another victim to conceal their identities.”
At their peak, the men had 10 computers running cryptomining software, according to indictments.
The Justice Department has increased the tempo of arrests and indictments of cybercriminals as nations have grown more willing to extradite those accused of cybercrimes.
Last week, two well-known Ghanaian cybercriminals pleaded guilty to charges related to their management of an international criminal organization that stole more than $100 million from victims via romance scams and business email compromises.
The two were part of a group extradited from Ghana last year after nearly a decade of cyberattacks on U.S. businesses.

articles.title: Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?
articles.snippet: Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder's web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.
articles.full_text:
Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.
The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.
The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications. Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.
There are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer.
Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight.
Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.
“This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote. “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.”
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover and other cybercrime activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.
They can also introduce serious security risks. In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local network for vulnerable systems to infect with malware. In January 2026, dozens of proxy services were forced to patch their networks after Synthient Founder Ben Brundage showed how cybercriminals were abusing a vulnerability in these residential proxy services to seize control over devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting users.
“Some of these resellers sell bandwidth for as low as 60 cents a Gigabyte, that means for less than a dollar you can gain access into some of the most confidential and trusted networks,” Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity. “The reseller ecosystem further enables this with any criminal able to buy access while skipping KYC [Know Your Customer] processes.”
All too often, these proxy services are beaconing out from employee devices brought into the workplace. App developers can embed software development kits (SDKs) provided by the residential proxy networks to monetize their software, allowing them to receive a small amount of money on each installation.
As risky as residential proxies can be for unsuspecting end users, they are all too commonly found on government and corporate networks. In a webinar in January 2026, the proxy tracking service Spur found residential proxies in nearly 300 government owned and operated networks, 318 utility companies, 166 healthcare companies or hospitals, and 141 companies in banking and finance. In a blog post earlier this year, the security firm Infoblox said it discovered that fully 65% of its customer base was querying one or more residential proxy related domains.
Incredible things happening in america rn
We may never know but I think that there are some staffers who forced the IT department to give them admin rights.
I’ve experienced that in a county courthouse. All of the judges had admin rights and the computers were set to never lock the screen. The county IT director allowed this.
Long time sysadmin here, tough to tell your boss no.
My last job was in healthcare, even with the HIPAA law (plus the HITECH changes) and training I would still see usernames and passwords written down all over the place. The owner and the CEO had laptops, which I kept telling them they needed to enable encryption on in case they were lost or stolen, would just shrug and ignore me.

articles.title: Tech Firms Dismantle Botnet That Turned 1.3M TV Boxes Into Proxies
articles.snippet: Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user's Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet's access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.
articles.full_text:
Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user’s Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet’s access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.
A report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said Google has severed ties with Videostrong Technology Co., a TV box manufacturer in China that GTIG and other industry experts concluded was responsible for including malware that enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet dubbed “XCPE” (named after one of the malware’s core code components).
The report said the XCPE botnet loaded the user’s device with software that makes their Internet address available for resale by multiple “residential proxy” services, which allow customers to rent Internet addresses as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.
“Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” the GTIG post reads, noting that Google took legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install additional malware. “A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors.”
The report notes that while TV boxes made up the the majority of the botnet, the same XCPE malware was found in other Android-based IoT products, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and even digital signage systems.
Google said it requires all Android device makers to pass compatibility and security tests to ensure their products don’t harm users, but that Videostrong nevertheless found a way to load their malicious software immediately after a user boots up one of these devices for the first time (Google says it has since addressed that weakness).
The GTIG report calls out a number of residential proxy providers whose software development kits were routinely downloaded by devices infected by the XCPE botnet. Those include AppSalt, also known as Honeygain, which was developed by the Vilnius, Lithuania-based Oxylabs. In October 2026, Oxylabs and Honeygain were reorganized as independent platforms under an umbrella entity called Source, which received $130 million in funding from private equity firm Warburg Pincus that reportedly valued the business at $3.6 billion.
Another provider linked to the botnet was NetNut, a once sprawling residential proxy company operated by the publicly-traded Israeli company Alarum Technologies. In July 2026, the FBI worked with industry partners to seize hundreds of domains associated with NetNut, saying the company was responsible for operating a separate botnet called Popa that enslaved TV boxes as residential proxies. Other proxy providers named in the GTIG report include EarnFM, Traffmonetizer, Jaguar, LINKFOG, BMW/IPWeb and GaGaNode.
Google’s announcement credits a number of industry partners, including Synthient, a startup that tracks proxy providers. In January 2026, Synthient published research into the rapid spread of the Kimwolf botnet, which at the time was hammering networks worldwide with record-smashing DDoS attacks. Synthient documented how Kimwolf infected millions of Android set-top boxes virtually overnight, using a widespread vulnerability in these residential proxy services to compromise other Android-based devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting TV box users.
Synthient’s research caused dozens of residential proxy providers to patch their networks, which helped to fragment the Kimwolf botnet into much smaller pieces that made its incessant and disruptive DDoS attacks far easier for network operators to manage. It also attracted the attention of the Motion Picture Association (MPA), a trade group representing the major Hollywood studios, which partnered with Synthient to purchase and tear apart a number of popular Android TV set-top boxes — including some that were being infected by Kimwolf and other IoT botnets.
In a report published today, Synthient examined a popular, pre-infected TV box sold under the brand MECOOL by a publicly traded company in China called Skyworth Technology, concluding that MECOOL also bundled the malware from Videostrong Technology Co. and likewise installed AppSalt/Honeygain and other proxy components.
Synthient founder Ben Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity that Videostrong’s malware also distributed software for the proxy service Grass. In our November 2025 story, “Is Your Android TV Streaming Box Part of a Botnet?” we quoted a researcher from Censys who found the popular Superbox TV streaming device bundled Grass’s residential proxy software. We also quoted the Grass founder, who denied any affiliation with the TV box maker.
That November 2025 story noted that Superbox and similar Android TV set-top boxes gain new customers primarily by engaging influencers on Tiktok and other social networks who praise the product’s ability to offer hundreds of (pirated) pay TV streaming services for a one-time fee.
Likewise, Synthient’s report observes that the MECOOL set-top boxes exploded in popularity after the product was mentioned in 2023 by the Youtube channel Linus Tech Tips, which has an audience of nearly 17 million subscribers [Linus Tech Tips said in a statement shared with Synthient that it has since updated the video to explicitly frame the product as a scam and have removed all associated affiliate links].
The GTIG report estimates the XCPE botnet takedown should sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices, noting that the various proxy and ad fraud affiliates of Videostrong “each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE.”
Synthient’s Brundage echoed that conclusion, calling the 1.3 million number “highly conservative.”
“The scale of affected devices is likely way higher,” he said. “This is probably the largest operation against backdoored TV boxes that we’ve seen.”
Update, Nov. 5, 11:07 a.m. ET: In a statement shared post-publication, Oxylabs said that while its system is built so that a device can’t be used as a proxy exit node unless they receive a signal that it has consented, the developer faked these signals.
“We have been conducting regular audits of the applications provided by our partners,” the statement reads. “However, following this incident, we will improve the application and application’s build fingerprinting logic to better detect cases where the SDK is running on an unapproved build of an originally authorized application.”
The statement said Oxylabs has no record of any company called Videostrong Technology Co., but it did find between is suppliers the domain “com.abc[.]nexus,” mentioned in the GTIG report as an external malware loader.
“As soon as we saw that, we suspended the relationship and sent them a formal legal inquiry,” the statement reads. “This supplier accounts for less than 1% of our IP address pool. We had a signed contract with them, they assured our QA team that users had given consent, and we saw the consent flow ourselves.”
